title: Who's on the Bills' roster bubble? 14 players fighting for the final spots Receivers Mecole Hardman and Trent Sherfield and tight end Keleki Latu are a few notable Bills on the bubble to make the 53-man roster. Joe Buscaglia

The Buffalo Bills will conclude their 2026 preseason against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night at Highmark Stadium.

full_text:
Trent Sherfield has been a steady presence and trusted voice in the Bills' wide receiver room this summer. Nick Cammett / Diamond Images via Getty Images
The Buffalo Bills will conclude their 2026 preseason against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night at Highmark Stadium.
It’s the last gasp for the fringes of the team to make the 53-man roster, either in Buffalo or elsewhere.
This year’s group is setting up to be one of the more difficult puzzles for Bills general manager Brandon Beane to solve, as the bubble is muddled across the roster. As the Bills prepare for cutdown day on Aug. 30, who are truly the bubble players with a lot on the line this week?
Here is our annual Bills bubble watch, and how the Bills roster stands with just a handful of days remaining for decisions.
The competition between rookie Tommy Doman Jr. and Mitch Wishnowsky has gotten tighter in recent days. After racing out to an early lead, Doman struggled with his last two punts against the Cleveland Browns on Saturday, and his practice on Tuesday was not up to his early-camp standard. While Doman’s still likely to win the job, it’s not the slam dunk it was earlier in August.
Bowry is a lock if healthy for the 53-man roster, but he suffered an injury in Cleveland and was in a walking boot to begin the practice week. The Bills have 12 players they could consider to make the team along the offensive line, but keeping that many doesn’t match the needs of the rest of the roster. For what it’s worth, head coach Joe Brady said that he didn’t think any of the current injuries change the roster math for them. However, considering stashing someone they want to keep on injured reserve has been a staple of Beane’s tenure, it would be unwise to rule it out — especially with the reserve OL roster crunch.
Allen ended any lingering backup debate in Cleveland. Ever since Connor McGovern went down with an injury, Cushenberry has been glued to the first-team offense and working with Josh Allen. Grable is trending toward being their top reserve swing tackle to begin 2026. Solomon and Andreessen have yet again established themselves as two of their best special teams assets. Hamlin has been their best backup safety so far this summer.
Hardman’s best path to the 53-man roster is as the primary punt returner, because his skill set on offense and how little they would use it really doesn’t justify keeping him. It doesn’t help that the Bills’ current wide receiver injuries to Khalil Shakir and Keon Coleman both seem to be trending positively toward Week 1. In recent weeks, Hardman has been challenged by backup running back and kickoff returner Ray Davis for the punt returner job, and Davis has come a long way in fielding punts. On top of that, Hardman did not practice Tuesday, which could mean a poorly timed injury.
Sherfield shined against the Browns, and all summer he’s been a steady presence and trusted voice in the wide receiver room. The real debate is whether the Bills need to carve out a spot on their 53-man roster for Sherfield, with fears he might head elsewhere. Sherfield is not subject to waivers, so he could be a clear practice squad stash and call-up when an injury calls for it.
Latu played really well at the beginning of training camp and has faded a bit over the last couple of weeks, but he does enough to warrant at least some consideration for the 53-man roster. His best chance to make it is if they decide not to carry the next position.
This summer, the Bills were attempting to figure out two things at fullback. First, which of their two fullbacks would have the best chance to make the 53-man roster. VanSumeren answered that after the Bills cut undrafted rookie Jackson Acker. Second, since it’s such a small offensive role, they had to decide whether keeping a fullback on the roster was necessary. While VanSumeren has to look good in those reps, being an almost every-phase special teams piece is just as important. If the Bills feel VanSumeren is that, he’s got a solid chance, but it’s still up in the air.
Heading into the summer, Reed-Adams was a bit of an afterthought as a seventh-round pick likely destined for the practice squad. However, his play in preseason games and recently during practices has changed the discussion. With four years of full roster control, the Bills may not want to risk a young player who has shown real potential in an NFL hungry for developmental talent. Reed-Adams is a guard only, which may hurt his chances for the 53-man roster because it could make him more likely to clear waivers. However, he is one of the most interesting names to monitor this weekend.
The 2024 fifth-round pick came into the summer hoping to solidify his hold on the backup center job but seems to have lost it outright to the veteran Cushenberry. For that reason, Van Pran-Granger is one of the true pivot points in their 53-man roster decisions, as he’s shown some good progress this summer despite losing the role. He’s got two years left on his rookie deal, and when Beane does deal away his former picks, it’s more likely to happen after their third camp and beyond.
Van Pran-Granger is a clear candidate for just that, as teams like the Minnesota Vikings, Washington Commanders, and some others are in real need of depth at center. Other than the trade route, Van Pran-Granger has not practiced the last two days, so perhaps the Bills can stash Van Pran-Granger on IR rather than lose another player at another position.
Of the many reserve offensive linemen the Bills spent a draft pick on in the last three years, Lundt has seen his stock worsen as the summer has continued. He’s played almost exclusively at guard recently, and the tape has been inconsistent. Of all their options, he might have the worst chance of the bunch to make the team, but I wouldn’t rule out a practice squad return.
First, Phidarian Mathis took reps from Carter, and now it’s Greg Gaines. No matter what, it’s pretty clear that the Bills were looking to strengthen their nose tackle rotation behind starter Deone Walker, which might be bad news for Carter. They have been very complimentary of Carter’s play, though him playing deep into the fourth quarter against the Browns could be meaningful. Carter may be a better fit for a 4-3 scheme. Then again, they could keep Carter and try to get Gaines on the practice squad. Regardless, keep Carter on your trade radar.
The Bills brought in Gaines less than a week ago, and usual NFL deduction skills point to a late veteran addition like this one usually meaning the team wants to keep them on the 53-man roster. Whether it follows that path remains to be seen, though it’s somewhat notable that after just a few days with the Bills, Gaines was already a part of the same early-game rotation as Carter against the Browns, and the team didn’t use Gaines at all in the second half.
A post-draft signing, Danna brought some experience to the outside linebacker room. At that point, the Bills had no idea if Michael Hoecht would be available to start the season. With Hoecht looking like a certainty to be healthy enough for Week 1, Danna may be on the outside looking in, as Solomon is the superior special teams player. It will come down to numbers at other positions.
Jenkins was a standout during training camp and ascended on the depth chart, though his preseason games may have slightly hurt his chances of making the 53-man roster. Without question, he is one of the names that will be among their most difficult calls of the summer. It likely won’t be Jenkins against someone else at his position, but rather either an additional offensive lineman or a depth defender. It could be a 50-50 call.
The undrafted rookie Walker has played himself into 53-man roster contention. He’s physical, he’s long-limbed, and he showed he’s got some real instincts for the position. Walker also played for Bills cornerbacks coach Jay Valai for three years at Oklahoma, which will certainly help his chances. The questionable…

full_text:
Shedeur Sanders celebrates during the second quarter of Saturday's preseason loss against the Bills. Jason Miller / Getty Images
The path to any future for Shedeur Sanders in Cleveland is narrowing. I can’t say it has completely vanished because I have no faith that Deshaun Watson can stay healthy for an entire season or be productive enough to keep the job.
The decision to name Watson the starter leaves a fair question worth exploring: What does this mean for Sanders?
If he has an NFL future past this season, it likely won’t be with the Browns.
By giving the starting job to Watson , a quarterback who hasn’t been consistently good since the pandemic, the Browns told you exactly what they think of Sanders. He had a full offseason program, OTAs, minicamp and training camp, and he still wasn’t good enough to beat out a quarterback the organization knows a) isn’t very good anymore and b) will be voraciously hissed and booed every time he’s on the field in Cleveland unless his play again resembles that of a productive NFL quarterback, which isn’t likely.
And they chose to do this anyway.
Browns coach Todd Monken did his best to prop up Sanders this summer and praise him for the progress he’s made as an NFL quarterback. Given where Sanders started, it was impossible to go down.
That Sanders has struggled with the most basic parts of being an NFL quarterback — the operational side of calling the play in the huddle, breaking the huddle quickly, getting guys lined up, speaking a cadence loudly and clearly enough for his linemen to hear him — is an indication of how far he has to travel if this is ever going to work. We haven’t even gotten to his processing times and how long he holds the ball (improved over last year, still not good enough).
If the Browns believed in Sanders, he would be starting Week 1. If they believed in him, there would’ve been no need to trade Myles Garrett because they would be operating as if the franchise quarterback was already on the roster.
Over the last two years, among 78 qualifying quarterbacks, Shedeur Sanders' 2025 performance ranked 77th in EPA per pass play.
The only performance that was worse statistically? Deshaun Watson's 2024, which ranked 78th.
— Sheil Kapadia (@SheilKapadia) August 24, 2026
Instead, the Browns keep telling their fans, without actually telling them, that their next quarterback is in the 2027 draft.
If that’s the case, there isn’t a place in the quarterback room for Sanders beyond this year. There is no logical world in which Sanders can be a backup to a rookie quarterback next year in Cleveland.
Backup quarterbacks are supposed to be anonymous until they’re needed. Sanders might be the most famous backup in football. Every interception by a rookie would turn into a referendum. Every losing streak would bring demands for Sanders. Every decision not to play Sanders would become another national debate about whether the Browns were treating him fairly. No organization should intentionally build that environment around a rookie quarterback it just drafted to save the franchise. Fair or not, the noise that surrounds Sanders creates an unhealthy environment for everyone else. His level of celebrity makes the normal developmental QB path for him incredibly difficult, particularly with an organization that hasn’t successfully developed a quarterback in 30 years.
The idea that Sanders could work in Cleveland was always far-fetched once it became clear how much development he had ahead . It will be nearly impossible starting next year if there is another high pick in the room.
Which leads back to: What are we doing here? It all feels like an enormous waste of time.
I’d love to write that the Browns should just cut Sanders and move on with their lives (he has little to no trade value right now), which is what I wrote at one point last season. But after an offseason of inactivity by the Browns at the game’s most important position, I can’t get there now because of how dreadful we know Watson has been and probably will continue to be.
Since Watson arrived in Cleveland, NFL quarterbacks have thrown for at least 300 yards on 481 occasions. Even Sanders is on that list. The quarterback who isn’t?
It’s hard to take the Browns seriously until they solve the quarterback position . To this point, they haven’t.
Sanders is simultaneously not good enough for the Browns to trust and, at least at the moment, too necessary for them to discard.
He will likely get another chance at some point this season. It’s possible he finishes with more QB starts than anyone else on Cleveland’s roster. Can he become good enough over the next four months to stop the Browns from using their most valuable resources on another quarterback in the spring?
All of their actions suggest the Browns already know the answer. The most important quarterback in Cleveland’s future is the one who isn’t here yet.

full_text:
There's a wide range of potential outcomes for the Kansas City Chiefs as Patrick Mahomes returns from an ACL injury. Cooper Neill / Getty Images
Last season represented the first time in 10 tries that the Kansas City Chiefs didn’t claim the AFC West crown.
The Denver Broncos were on the right side of “luck,” going 11-2 in one-score games to end the Chiefs’ reign, who were on the less fortunate side of that coin with a 1-9 record in such games.
It’s shaping up to be another interesting race in 2026, with sportsbooks like DraftKings listing odds that imply the Broncos, Chiefs and Los Angeles Chargers each have around a 30 percent chance to win the division title. Here’s a closer look at the board as well as how my model forecasts every AFC West team’s season — including why the projections mirror the expectations of books.
This is the best and deepest division in the AFC, hence why there’s no runaway favorite.
To take it a step farther: The Chargers, who my model rates as the best of the bunch, face the fifth-hardest schedule in the NFL. The Chiefs are contending with a fair amount of uncertainty with Patrick Mahomes returning from an ACL injury and questions on defense. And my model believes the Broncos’ 2025 season was quite fortunate and is thus expecting regression.
All of these factors combine to net each team winning the division about 30 percent of the time. And while each has a high ceiling, they also come with a decently low floor.
The Chargers dealt with offensive line injuries last year and are already contenting with some this year: Center Tyler Biadasz is out for the season with a knee injury, and offensive tackle Rashawn Slater isn’t 100 percent just yet. New offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel probably gives them the highest ceiling in the division, but if the offensive line isn’t healthy, it’s going to be tough sledding once again.
Another team with a high ceiling, the Chiefs are also dealing with uncertainty at offensive tackle as well as in the secondary. And even if Mahomes is fully healthy, the roster doesn’t have bulletproof talent — the past two Super Bowls have been won with great rosters, and I’m not sure the Chiefs are in that position.
Now for the defending division champion Broncos. You might be surprised to see them projected to finish third, but should we really be shocked if they regress on the backs of an offense that ranked in the bottom-third of the league in 2025? That’s why I can’t get too excited about Denver. Yes, adding wide receiver Jaylen Waddle is super intriguing and should help. But if this is just an average offense, are we sure that double-digit wins are in order given the talent in this division?
After taking everything into account, you end up with three good football teams that all have their own blemishes playing in a quality division. That’s going to put three teams around 9-10 wins with enough uncertainty to give them all an equal chance to win the AFC West.

full_text:
Jordan Love was all smiles before the Packers' preseason game against the Broncos this month. (Jamie Schwaberow / Getty Images) Jamie Schwaberow / Getty Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — J. Michael Sturdivant’s first interaction with Jordan Love surprised him.
Sturdivant, an undrafted rookie wide receiver from Florida, was in the Lambeau Field weight room this spring when Love, the $220 million franchise quarterback and one of the NFL’s best at his position, walked in.
“He came up calling me by my first name,” said Sturdivant, whom everyone calls “J-Mike.” “That kind of threw me off because I didn’t think he even knew who I was.”
Sturdivant has been one of the Packers’ training camp standouts, making a convincing case for his inclusion on the 53-man roster. Folks inside and outside 1265 Lombardi Ave. are probably more familiar with him now, but few should’ve been early in his Packers tenure since they didn’t even use a draft pick on him.
Love was, however, and such a mundane interaction offered a glimpse into who Love is when cameras are off and why he’s so respected inside the locker room as the leader of the pack — pun intended.
“Being able to get close to a guy like that and be able to talk to him — when I first got here, I was eating breakfast with him and Tucker Kraft every day,” Sturdivant said. “So seeing how humble and how willing those guys were to speak to somebody that just got in the building when I was an undrafted rookie, it was kind of cool.”
Sturdivant is hardly the only player fighting for a spot on the Packers with a story like that about Love.
Cornerback Jaylin Simpson, a third-year player on the roster bubble who’s played in one career game, often played ping-pong with Love at a table in the middle of the locker room when reporters were in there this offseason. Simpson even took the emcee’s mic at Love’s charity softball game in June to trash his quarterback’s ping-pong skills.
They’d play a best-of-three series every other day during the offseason and, shockingly, Simpson said he’s better.
“I’m pretty sure I won the last game, and you’re only as good as your last game, so I’m the winner,” Simpson said early in training camp. “Bunch of the times I won two games in a row, so he didn’t even get a chance to play a third one.”
By the end of Aaron Rodgers’ career in Green Bay, it seemed everyone knew everything about him, perhaps thanks to his weekly appearances on the “Pat McAfee Show.” Love has endeared himself to Packers fans thanks to his play over three seasons as the starting quarterback, but he comes off as more subdued than his predecessor and perhaps shrouded in a bit more mystery, since Love doesn’t always show his personality publicly as Rodgers did.
One thing they share, besides tremendous right-arm talent, is their penchant for good deeds behind closed doors. Rodgers sought out young players at the lunch table to get to know them, stopped a tryout player and his mom on their drive out of Lambeau Field to give him props and gave Keisean Nixon a hug when he first arrived in 2022 (Nixon hated hugs) to help turn Nixon from someone who hated Green Bay to the opposite.
During training camp in 2024, Love was part of a small group that accompanied former Packers center Josh Myers on a private jet to his father’s funeral in Ohio. He’s continued to earn the respect of guys who go to battle for him, no matter their standing on the team.
“As a guy who’s practice squad, who just hasn’t contributed a lot to the team, he makes you feel like you are contributing a lot to the team, like y’all besties,” Simpson said. “I love J-Love. He makes you feel good.”
“It doesn’t matter who you are, where you are on the depth chart or anything like that. He sees you on the side of the street, he’s probably gonna talk to you,” said 2025 undrafted wide receiver Will Sheppard.
Isaiah Neyor is another Packers wideout on the roster bubble this summer. He signed on Aug. 6 last year as an undrafted rookie. Eight days later, Love pulled him aside during a joint practice with the Indianapolis Colts.
“I had made a few plays, and I thought I did something good, but he came up to me,” Neyor said. “He congratulated me, but he told me, like, ‘Ay, man.’ He was talking to me about my (route) stem or something like that, just kinda working on that and keeping my angle right. So just him doing that alone, even just the smallest of things, hearing that from somebody like him, it definitely means a lot.
“That alone gives me confidence. ‘OK, if Jordan Love is coming up to me, he has high expectations for me,’ so that gives me confidence going out on the field to know that he believes in me to do what I need to do. … He talks to everybody the same, whether you’re a starter, second-, third-string, whatever the case may be. He treats everybody the same, and that’s what makes him who he is.”
Before every practice, Love conducts custom handshakes with each running back, from feature back Josh Jacobs to undrafted rookie Jaden Nixon, who might be last on the six-man depth chart.
Nixon was caught off guard on his first day at Lambeau Field when Love wanted to create a handshake with him.
“I said, ‘We got a handshake ?’” Nixon recalled. “He was like, ‘Yeah, we gotta come up with something.’”
They settled on something simple — one slap of the front of their hands, one of the back, and then two more with the front before covering their face with their hand and doing a little dance.
“I don’t know,” Nixon said. “I just randomly made it up one day.”
Jordan Love’s custom handshakes with all five running backs pic.twitter.com/uv7t7Q21PC
— Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) August 2, 2026
Nixon showed genuine excitement talking about this handshake inside the locker room. He stuck his tongue out and made a noise to demonstrate what their dance entails and even had me do the handshake with him.
“When you see a star quarterback like him, that franchise player, the head honcho, it’s like, ‘OK, I’m just a scrub to him,’ you know what I mean?” Nixon said. “As long as I’m not in his way, I’m good. It’s kinda like those old Disney movies where it’s like, don’t mess with the jock, the superstar of the team. But he doesn’t seem like that. He’s just (a) cool, goofy, energetic dude who’s down to earth.”
Fourth-string running back Pierre Strong Jr. said he and Love have an inside joke about whose hair is longer.
“If he wasn’t in this building and he changed his name — he acts like he’s an average guy,” Strong said. “You wouldn’t even think he’s No. 1, made all these millions. … I love him, and he’s like a brother to me.”
MJ Devonshire, perhaps the No. 9 cornerback, said Love has given even him confidence as a third-year player potentially fighting for even a spot on the practice squad.
“When you do something good, he’ll make sure he’ll come up to you and let you know you made a good play or just after practice, dap you up. ‘Good job out there today,’” Devonshire said. “Just making you feel noticed, like everyone’s on this team. Whatever you doing, if you showing up on film, he’s gon’ make sure he lets you know that you showing up on film. So whenever I do something, him being there and saying something to me is definitely an important thing for my confidence.”
Some quarterbacks might have a “C” on their chest because they’re quarterbacks.
Love has earned that honor through both his play and how he treats people inside the building.
Does being a great teammate directly lead to wins? Of course not. It only matters so much. But it’s easier to put your body on the line for someone like Love, who’s perhaps the most beloved member of the locker room for more than his position.

full_text:
First-team All-Pro defensive end Will Anderson Jr. is among eight Texans defensive starters returning for a third straight year. Alex Slitz / Getty Images
The Los Angeles Rams have assembled a super team that could be capped by the return of Aaron Donald, but they’ll have several players playing together for the first time, and cohesion isn’t guaranteed. The Seattle Seahawks are the defending champions but have lost two key members of their secondary in free agency and their second-round pick, safety Bud Clark, who was supposed to be a replacement for Coby Bryant, broke an ankle in the preseason.
The Rams and Seahawks could very well finish with the top defenses this season, but the Houston Texans have a strong case to finish first and be a historically memorable unit. The defense alone is dominant enough to make the Texans playoff contenders, and with improvement from the offense in its second year in coordinator Nick Caley’s system, they are legitimate Super Bowl contenders.
The Texans’ defense is keeping a core of eight together for the third year in a row, playing in the same system, which rarely happens in the salary-cap era. Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter make up the best edge duo in the league. Derek Stingley Jr., Kamari Lassiter and nickel Jalen Pitre are the best cornerback trio in the league. Linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair fits this system perfectly, and though he can step over the line, he personifies this defense’s attitude. Safety Calen Bullock and linebacker Henry To’o To’o aren’t household names, but they round out the eight.
After the Texans finished second to the Seahawks in points allowed per drive (1.48), where does their defense improve? Defensive coordinator Matt Burke, to whom coach DeMeco Ryans handed play-calling duties last season, said they Texans entered the offseason looking to reduce explosive passes and improve in the red zone.
“I think we had one drive all year that we gave a touchdown on that didn’t have an explosive,” Burke said. “It’s pretty hard to score on us if you’re not generating explosive plays like that.”
The Texans ranked in the top five in nearly every major category last season, but they ranked 16th in explosive passes allowed (passes of 20 yards or more). Twenty of their 78 explosive pass plays allowed came against man coverage. They didn’t play a ton of man — they ranked No. 18 in percentage of man played, but an issue could be that they don’t try to disguise when they do.
This presnap look was on Kayshon Boutte’s touchdown against the Texans in the playoffs. The defense showed blitz and single-high with pressed corners, so Drake Maye knew exactly where to go with the ball before the snap.
This is an easy fix. The benefit of having the same players in the system is that layers can be added. The defense has a reputation for keeping its menu limited and playing fast but is a lot more varied than it gets credit for. Burke said the Texans are also working on eliminating miscommunications, improvement that, again, can come with time together. For example, on third down, they lead the league in Cover 6 usage — a two-high coverage usually associated with Vic Fangio-influenced defenses.
The Texans play two deep safeties at the 12th-highest rate in the league. Teams that use this scheme typically play more passively up front. They want their defensive line to control the gaps to make ballcarriers run outside so their secondary has time to come up and help. Teams using an attacking style usually have to keep an extra safety in the box to account for every gap. The Texans have been able to remain sound against the run, keeping two safeties back and attacking up front.
“Our belief system is that we want to be disruptive up front in attacking, and we don’t want to read blocks,” Burke explained. “And so when you have to run fit out the second level or behind that, that’s how you develop your coverage process, what fits with that front and how we can play. So there’s certain ways we can adjust that.”
Unlike many modern coverages that have the defensive line play a certain style to provide flexibility in coverage, the Texans’ coverage system is built around allowing their front to attack.
“Honestly, having someone like (Jalen) Pitre as a nickel, who can still be a good run player when he’s out in space and apex, is key,” Burke said. “And then, obviously, having enough changeups up front and disguises. So you just build (the system) out where you’re not just sitting on one thing, one coverage, one front, like that’s not how we play, either. There’s enough wrinkles, there’s a lot of good players. Again, our starting point for our front is we want to be disruptive and attack, and we don’t want to alter that.”
Here, the Texans lined up with two deep safeties, with Pitre in the nickel. He was apexed but looked to be responsible for playing the B gap.
The Seahawks had a trap play called, which is a common answer for attacking fronts. The play looked as if it was set up perfectly. Pitre was still outside the box as the running back was getting the handoff.
In the blink of an eye, however, Pitre flew across the front and made a tackle for a minimal gain.
Everything is built around the defensive line. Burke said the Texans even use one-word defensive play calls so the line can deploy quickly and get into the right mindset at the line of scrimmage rather than hurry if they spend too much time in the defensive huddle.
This is the Legion of Boom for the modern era. Offensive coaches have made Pete Carroll’s Seahawks system obsolete, but Ryans and Burke have updated it. It’s a unique look for offenses to have to game plan against.
Outside of scheme, the Texans play with a desire to destroy. They fly off the line of scrimmage and swarm to the ball. Part of it is culture, and part of it is that they look for a little frenzy when bringing in players.
“You’ll hear DeMeco say, ‘This isn’t for everyone.’ The way we play … the way we practice,” Burke said at camp last week. “It’s been a long day out here today, right? Not everyone is built for that, and that’s OK. When we try to identify players to acquire, we’re very intentional in the types of people that we bring in so that they fit that style.
“And then I would say, the way that we teach our front, talk about our front and the way we play … there’s a natural built-in aggressiveness to how we play, and so that sort of feeds into that stylistically throughout the rest of defense.”
The offense must exude that mentality for the Texans to be contenders. They drafted interior lineman Keylan Rutledge with their first-round pick and traded for David Montgomery, a sledgehammer of a running back. Woody Marks even looked as if he’s become a more physical runner in joint practice against the Las Vegas Raiders. The Texans signed blocking tight end Foster Moreau and drafted tight end Marlin Klein in the second round to complement Dalton Schultz. The Texans were intent on adding big bodies and physicality on offense.
The Texans ranked No. 30 in rushing success rate last season and No. 24 in explosive rush rate (runs of 12-plus yards). In 2024, they ranked last in rushing success rate, and in 2023 (quarterback C.J. Stroud’s rookie year), they ranked No. 25. The Texans have never given Stroud an efficient running game. To make matters worse, they ranked No. 30 in pass-block win rate last season, and they’ve had one of the most injured receiving corps since he’s been in the league. Jayden Higgins, who was expected to be the Texans’ No. 2 receiver this season, tore an ACL in the joint practice against the Raiders.
The lack of help doesn’t take the onus off Stroud or absolve him of turning the ball over seven times in the playoffs last season, but he’s been fighting an uphill battle. Losing Higgins hurts, but the Texans are more equipped to handle it this season and should be more of a tight end-oriented offense even after trading for Boutte .

full_text:
There's a wide range of potential outcomes for the Kansas City Chiefs as Patrick Mahomes returns from an ACL injury. Cooper Neill / Getty Images
Last season represented the first time in 10 tries that the Kansas City Chiefs didn’t claim the AFC West crown.
The Denver Broncos were on the right side of “luck,” going 11-2 in one-score games to end the Chiefs’ reign, who were on the less fortunate side of that coin with a 1-9 record in such games.
It’s shaping up to be another interesting race in 2026, with sportsbooks like DraftKings listing odds that imply the Broncos, Chiefs and Los Angeles Chargers each have around a 30 percent chance to win the division title. Here’s a closer look at the board as well as how my model forecasts every AFC West team’s season — including why the projections mirror the expectations of books.
This is the best and deepest division in the AFC, hence why there’s no runaway favorite.
To take it a step farther: The Chargers, who my model rates as the best of the bunch, face the fifth-hardest schedule in the NFL. The Chiefs are contending with a fair amount of uncertainty with Patrick Mahomes returning from an ACL injury and questions on defense. And my model believes the Broncos’ 2025 season was quite fortunate and is thus expecting regression.
All of these factors combine to net each team winning the division about 30 percent of the time. And while each has a high ceiling, they also come with a decently low floor.
The Chargers dealt with offensive line injuries last year and are already contenting with some this year: Center Tyler Biadasz is out for the season with a knee injury, and offensive tackle Rashawn Slater isn’t 100 percent just yet. New offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel probably gives them the highest ceiling in the division, but if the offensive line isn’t healthy, it’s going to be tough sledding once again.
Another team with a high ceiling, the Chiefs are also dealing with uncertainty at offensive tackle as well as in the secondary. And even if Mahomes is fully healthy, the roster doesn’t have bulletproof talent — the past two Super Bowls have been won with great rosters, and I’m not sure the Chiefs are in that position.
Now for the defending division champion Broncos. You might be surprised to see them projected to finish third, but should we really be shocked if they regress on the backs of an offense that ranked in the bottom-third of the league in 2025? That’s why I can’t get too excited about Denver. Yes, adding wide receiver Jaylen Waddle is super intriguing and should help. But if this is just an average offense, are we sure that double-digit wins are in order given the talent in this division?
After taking everything into account, you end up with three good football teams that all have their own blemishes playing in a quality division. That’s going to put three teams around 9-10 wins with enough uncertainty to give them all an equal chance to win the AFC West.

full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — Garrett Wilson longs for the kind of football he grew up watching. He thinks about the Sundays on his father’s couch in Austin, Texas. He’d watch the wide receivers and marvel at what they could do.
Even now, he still thinks about the life Terrell Owens got to live as a star wide receiver. Things were simpler then. If a coach had Terrell Owens, he’d build his offense around getting the ball to Terrell Owens.
“Guys like that, you don’t see as much anymore because it’s more schematic now,” Wilson told The Athletic . “It doesn’t have to be. That’s what it moved toward, but it doesn’t have to be.”
Modern offenses, he says, have become overcomplicated, bright-eyed masterminds trying to show everyone how smart they are. Wilson thinks they sometimes fail to see what’s right in front of them. “With receivers like Terrell Owens, his coaches knew they had a special talent,” Wilson says. “We’re not going to overcomplicate it. It’s man coverage, let’s throw a fade to Terrell Owens. The last 10 years you’ve seen that fall off and it’s all about everyone’s plays.”
To Wilson, early days with New York Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich have felt like a blast from that past. Reich is coaching the kind of football Wilson always dreamed of playing. He felt it from their first conversation, when Reich had clearly already studied him, understood which routes and plays best suited his skill set, and shared his plan to deploy the star receiver. He showed Wilson film of other wide receivers to come through Reich’s offense, like T.Y. Hilton with the Indianapolis Colts and Alshon Jeffery with the Philadelphia Eagles. He’d be showing old clips, but in an offense that Wilson sees as timeless.
“When he’s pulling clips up to show us examples, some of the clips are from like 2014 or ’15, and he don’t gotta say anything, but we all notice it. The clip is blurry as hell,” Wilson says. “This isn’t a complicated game, and I think Frank gets that. The schemes that have worked for a while will work.”
This isn’t a complicated game.
Wilson sees Reich calling aspects of an offense that simply — there’s that word again — uses “five good players” running routes designed to win versus man coverage or Cover 3.
“You don’t gotta recreate the wheel,” Wilson says.
“That’s the league I grew up watching and loving. That’s the receivers I grew up watching. That’s what it was. Frank reminds me of the league that I grew up watching.”
Reich walks into a meeting room and looks … lighter. He’s no longer carrying the weight of being a head coach. Jelani Woods has seen it. The tight end laughs in team meetings sometimes, looking around, thinking about how this is the only version of Reich his Jets teammates have ever experienced.
Reich was Woods’ first NFL head coach, the one who drafted him in 2022 with the Indianapolis Colts. That was at the end of his tenure, when things were a bit more tense than they’d been at the beginning. Reich was fired midway through that season. The coach had always carried himself with a level of grace and professionalism, but Woods never saw him particularly loose. Back then, Woods saw him as “stern” and “strict” — not in a bad way, but not exactly the Energizer Bunny.
When Woods was a rookie, Reich put a lot of work into getting him ready for the NFL. He was hard on him. “He was on me,” Woods says.
“Frank is a little different now. Frank then, he was a head coach so it’s a little different mindset. He still has some of that now, but he’s not leading the whole team, just the offense. Now he’s still stern — but he’s a little more laid back. I can see the fun he’s having. I can see the joy in him again.”
Reich was fired and replaced by Jeff Saturday midway through that 2022 season. He was fired again in an even more dysfunctional situation, with the Carolina Panthers a year later. That experience — with a meddling owner questioning his decisions at every turn — dimmed some of the light he had carried with him as a beloved and respected NFL figure since his playing days.
The plan was to retire until Andrew Luck came calling, asking Reich to take over as Stanford’s interim head coach for the 2025 season. Reich would coach for one last season, then sail off into the sunset. Instead, even in a 4-8 season, Reich felt his football itch once again. When the opportunity expired, he was open to returning to the NFL, but he wasn’t going to just take any job. He turned down some opportunities with close NFL friends, like a job working with Eagles coach Nick Sirianni.
That’s when Aaron Glenn called. The two were teammates 30 years ago for a 1-15 Jets team led by Rich Kotite, just before Bill Parcells arrived to change the culture and set a moribund franchise back on the right path. Glenn wanted his old friend to help him do the same thing.
“As soon as AG called, I knew right away this was something I wanted to do, mainly because of him, but also because of the challenge and the opportunity to be a part of a staff and be a part of a team and organization that has an opportunity to do something special and turn something around,” Reich said in May. “At this point, I love that idea and I’m excited about that, and I feel like I got something to offer.”
In the aftermath of a disastrous 3-14 debut season for Glenn, Reich checked in on him. He told Glenn to stay true to who he was as a man and as a football coach, to keep sticking with his process and to “not let anything on the outside deter you from what you’re trying to do.” Glenn said it was a meaningful conversation from someone he respects — and who understands the perils of an NFL head coach.
In Glenn’s debut season, he was so focused on being a CEO head coach that, he admits, he lost sight of what got him here in the first place. He hired a first-time offensive coordinator (Tanner Engstrand) and spent more time supervising that side of the ball than devoting his energy to building the defense in his image. The defense suffered as a result. So, when Glenn decided to fire Steve Wilks as defensive coordinator and eventually take back defensive play calling for himself, he wanted to hire an offensive play caller that didn’t require supervision, that had done that job before — that had done his job before.
Reich has said that opportunity reignited his fire. Everyone who comes in contact with him can feel that warmth.
“Every single unit meeting we have, he finds a way — I’m saying this for me because I’m a pretty chill, cool, composed guy — but by the end of every unit meeting, he has me feeling like I’m ready to run through a wall,” tackle Olu Fashanu says.
Says Woods: “He has so much energy now, so much joyfulness. It’s a sight to see.”
Jets wide receivers coach Shawn Jefferson, who was on Reich’s staff in Carolina, says Reich “has this presence about him that he’s able to draw people in” and that “every day he stands in front of that team, the guy is just dialed in. He sets the tempo every day for this offense. The players have really, really bought into his message.”
When Reich was hired, Adonai Mitchell — drafted by the Colts in 2024 — reached out to his old teammates about what to expect; wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. gave him a report. Breece Hall heard the same from Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor, a close friend.
“The first thing (Pittman) told me was: ‘You’re gonna love him,’ ” Mitchell says. “He’s a great coach, knows what he’s doing and has a great plan. Shoot, so I was ready.”
Taylor told Hall: “It’s very easy to play for Frank. He’s a very chill and cool dude, but he definitely wants you to execute what he’s telling you to do. He said he’s very easy to play for and he makes you play harder for him because of how good of a person he is, how good of a coach he is, how he’s a players’ coach and how he rides for his guys.”
Reich believes his fire comes from two places: Glenn and the Jets players he gets to work with.

full_text:
At 5 feet 11, Willie Lampkin is the shortest offensive lineman in the NFL. Scott Taetsch / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Willie Lampkin has been difficult to miss this summer. Well, that’s not totally true — when watching him in the huddle with the other offensive linemen, you might miss him.
But once the ball is snapped or there’s a one-on-one drill between linemen, you’ll notice Lampkin.
This summer, coaches reviewed practice film and shared a similar reaction.
“Man, Willie did it again,” Nick Sirianni said.
At (a listed) 5 feet 11 and 295 pounds, Lampkin is the shortest Eagles offensive lineman. He’s the NFL’s shortest offensive lineman. He’s the shortest offensive lineman on a roster since at least 2000, per TruMedia. Lampkin shares a position group in Philadelphia with the 6-9, 346-pound Markel Bell and the 6-8, 365-pound Jordan Mailata.
Yet Landon Dickerson calls him the Eagles’ “secret weapon.” Jordan Davis, who’s 6-6 and 336 pounds, calls him a “bowling ball of knives” and says facing Lampkin keeps him awake at night. Lampkin entered training camp on the roster bubble, but it’s hard to envision the Eagles putting the 53-man roster together this weekend without Lampkin’s name on it given how he’s played this summer. And he could be one of the Eagles’ top reserves on the interior offensive line, with the ability to fill in at center and guard.
Not that it should necessarily be a surprise. Lampkin’s football story is about suspending disbelief and acknowledging exceptions to prototypes. Somebody his size is not supposed to play offensive line the way he does until you accept that he can — and he does.
“What is he as a football player?” asked LeCharles Bentley, a two-time Pro Bowl offensive lineman and Lampkin’s performance coach, by phone this week. “Well, he has incredible balance, elite-level strength, extremely explosive, and a very high-level skill ability where you just watch him play the game. So if I just think through and say, ‘Well, what is it that as a football player you need, as an offensive lineman, as a guard, as a center, what do you need?’ All the things that you actually need, he checked those boxes. … He understands how to organize his body from a skill perspective to play the game.”
Bentley has worked with Lampkin for five seasons. Bentley is the founder of AMDG Sports, the agency that represents Lampkin. The question Bentley posed — “What is he as a football player?” — is the reason he started working with Lampkin in the first place. Bentley can tell you every center who’s ever made the Pro Football Hall of Fame down to how many were over 6-1 or 6-3. He knows Lampkin does not fit the NFL’s desired size requirements for the position. It’s why he warned Lampkin upon their first meeting that he would go undrafted. It’s hard for a league that creates parameters at positions to get behind the shortest player at his spot in recent memory. But he also knew what would happen once Lampkin arrived in a camp.
“All the things that you believe about him as a player … all these things that matter,” Bentley said. “So the limitation was going to be his height. Got it. But as a center, as a guard, is that really something that’s going to remove his ability to play football, because if I look at him in comparison to just to, say, a guard at 6-3 or a center that’s 6-3, well, Willie’s gonna test off the charts in comparison to that player’s strength level, that player’s explosion, certainly that player’s balance in his ability to organize his body and express skill. So technically, he’s a better football player. He’s just not 6-3. So how is that going to limit his ability to play the position and play the game? It doesn’t.”
Questions about his height have become old for Lampkin. They were old last season, when the Eagles claimed him off waivers after the Los Angeles Rams cut him with an injury and expected him to pass through to injured reserve. “I can’t change it,” Lampkin said of his size. But it’s hard to miss — especially for those who aren’t familiar with his story and are just learning about Lampkin for the first time.
He was a standout wrestler in high school who considered giving up football during his junior year at Lakeland (Fla.) High School. He went to Coastal Carolina, where he started his first three seasons before transferring to North Carolina. By his second year with the Tar Heels, he won the Jacobs Blocking Trophy as the ACC’s best offensive lineman.
He was a late addition to the Senior Bowl, where his strong showing made him a buzzy name in the scouting community but could not compel a team to draft him. The Rams signed him as an undrafted rookie and thought they would get him on IR without using a spot on the 53-man roster. Howie Roseman claimed him and used the roster spot before placing him on IR, where he spent his rookie season.
The first chance Lampkin had to participate in one-on-ones, he called on Jalen Carter and wanted to face the NFL’s highest-paid defensive tackle. That earned Carter’s respect. “He’s a dawg, man,” Carter said.
Teammates have taken notice of his proficiency. Lane Johnson pointed to Lampkin’s “excellent leverage” and said Lampkin is “really quick off the ball.” Once Lampkin gets his hands on a defensive lineman, Johnson said, “they rarely get him off.” Defensive tackle Byron Young said even though Lampkin is small, he can “engulf you” when he gets under the defender. Unless the defensive tackle can get arm extension on Lampkin, it’s going to be a win for Lampkin.
“It’s definitely a challenge seeing him when he comes in compared to a traditional-size offensive lineman,” Young said.
No other lineman on the Eagles measures shorter than 6-3 or weighs under 300 pounds. The defensive linemen get used to playing a certain way. Lampkin’s unorthodox size forces the defenders to adjust, and leverage is such a valuable tool at the line of scrimmage. Sometimes, the tallest linemen are affected by undersized players winning with leverage.
“He’s kind of like our secret weapon when it comes to the D-linemen,” Dickerson said. “I don’t think he’s your typical size for an offensive lineman, which can be a game changer going against a defensive lineman.”
“He’s so short, he’s so small, he’s so stubby, but he is so quick and powerful and precise with his hands,” Davis said. “For a taller guy like me, it gives me a lot of trouble, a lot of fits. It keeps me up at night with Willie. He’s a tremendous player. He has a certain tenacity about him.”
There comes a point when the Lampkin evaluation shifts from feel-good, underdog story to wondering how he could contribute in the NFL. One reason teams have size parameters is they cannot field a team of exceptions. In a deficient area, the exception is exposed, and to last, the exception must be exceptional somewhere else.
For Lampkin, that’s balance. It might not seem like an obvious skill. It’s hard to test at the combine. But Bentley, who excelled at the position, said Lampkin has the best balance in the league outside of Aaron Brewer.
Balance, explosion, strength, technique — he checks boxes in those areas. Bentley kept returning to the prevailing message: He has what’s needed to play football. He’s just not tall.
Does that lower his ceiling? Bentley, who’s listed at 6-2 and 309 pounds, remarked it’s not a position that requires great size. Of the centers in the Pro Football Hall of Fame, only one is 6-4. The rest are between 6-1 and 6-3. None of them is over 300 pounds. This was not to suggest Lampkin is a Hall of Famer. He’s not yet a starter, but there’s sometimes too much focus on the deficiency and not enough on the strengths.
Don’t take this to mean that every undersized center deserves a spot on NFL rosters. There might not be an enduring lesson to Lampkin’s story because every undersized center doesn’t have the other areas in his game. The same was true when Darren Sproles played for the Eagles. Lampkin could be more of an outlier than an example, but there’s little…

title: Should the Steelers keep four QBs? The pros and cons of an unorthodox roster move Pittsburgh is in an unusual position, with two developmental prospects behind two veterans. Mike DeFabo
summary:
The Steelers' four QBs, from left: Mason Rudolph, Drew Allar, Aaron Rodgers, Will Howard. Gene J. Puskar / Associated Press
The quarterback questions that have dominated Steelers training camp will soon be answered. Friday’s preseason game in Buffalo is expected to feature a heavy dose of Will Howard and Drew Allar. By 6 p.m. ET on Sunday, the 53-man roster is due and the final decision will be official.
How many quarterbacks will the Steelers keep, and how will they be ordered on the depth char
full_text:
The Steelers' four QBs, from left: Mason Rudolph, Drew Allar, Aaron Rodgers, Will Howard. Gene J. Puskar / Associated Press
The quarterback questions that have dominated Steelers training camp will soon be answered. Friday’s preseason game in Buffalo is expected to feature a heavy dose of Will Howard and Drew Allar. By 6 p.m. ET on Sunday, the 53-man roster is due and the final decision will be official.
How many quarterbacks will the Steelers keep, and how will they be ordered on the depth chart? Coach Mike McCarthy, publicly at least, said that the decision has not yet been made. However, when asked on Tuesday if he could find enough reps for four quarterbacks — Aaron Rodgers, Mason Rudolph, Howard and Allar — McCarthy appeared more than open to this possibility.
“I don’t think it would hinder (the opportunity to develop) at all,” McCarthy said. “We’ve talked extensively about the importance of the whole quarterback room. If you have four quarterbacks in that room, especially the quality that we have currently, I think it only enhances what the regular season would look like.”
McCarthy said that there are fewer time restrictions during the season under the CBA. In that way, he’d be able to do more with his QB School before and after practice than he’s permitted to currently.
“I’d have six quarterbacks in the building if it worked,” he said.
As the time nears to make the decision final, let’s take a look at the arguments for and against keeping four quarterbacks on the 53-man roster.
Shifting priorities toward the most important position: The Steelers’ inability to identify, draft and develop Ben Roethlisberger’s successor is a significant reason why the team hasn’t won a playoff game in almost a decade, why coach Mike Tomlin resigned and why the team pivoted from its defense-first model to hire an offensive-minded head coach in McCarthy. If the quarterback position was one of the main reasons the Steelers chose McCarthy, it would make sense to surround him with as many moldable pieces as possible.
A backup quarterback for now — and two for the future: Rather than turning over the roster when McCarthy was hired, the Steelers remained committed to the current window by keeping aging veterans such as T.J. Watt, extending 37-year-old Cameron Heyward, trading for a 28-year-old Michael Pittman Jr., adding a 29-year-old Jamel Dean and — more than anything else — waiting for a 42-year-old Rodgers. If the Steelers are going to put themselves in this win-now posture, Rudolph gives them the best chance to step in and win a game or two if Rodgers goes down with an injury. Carrying two young QB who have never appeared in an NFL regular season game behind a 42-year-old QB would be a risk.
Organizational belief in development: When the Steelers drafted Rudolph in 2018, they didn’t even employ a quarterbacks coach. Under McCarthy, the approach to QB development couldn’t be more different than what Rudolph went through. With his QB School, McCarthy is, arguably, the most hands-on head coach in the league when it comes to drilling the fundamentals. When you add in OC Brian Angelichio, QBs coach Tom Arth (who went through the QB school himself) and Rodgers, the Steelers have created an ideal environment for a young passer to learn.
Rodgers factor: Rodgers has proven himself to be a willing mentor from the moment he walked into the building a year ago. Allar talked about how the future Hall of Fame QB has given him “cheat codes” to beat certain coverages. Howard has discussed how Rodgers has helped him understand defenses on a much deeper level. In virtually every practice, Rodgers is giving the young quarterbacks some small piece of information — how to throw the ball on the run, how to carry out play-action, how to manipulate defenders with their eyes. Keeping both QBs would give them both the opportunity to learn all that Rodgers has to offer.
Setting the stage for 2027: The Steelers did everything in their power to put themselves in position to land a first-round quarterback in 2026, stockpiling a league-high 12 draft picks. However, when a once-promising QB class underperformed, it left the Steelers taking a chance in the middle rounds. So while it’s easy to say that right now the Steelers’ answer at QB can be found in the early rounds of the 2027 draft, what if they’re in the same situation as last year? Rodgers is likely to play well enough to keep the Steelers from picking early enough to get one of the top passers. By keeping Howard and Allar, the Steelers can develop the two young QBs this year and then have them compete for the starting job in 2027.
Kicks the can down the road: Right now, the decision appears to be Rudolph or Howard. Down the road, the Steelers have to pick between Howard and Allar. By keeping all four quarterbacks, the Steelers would be delaying that decision and hedging their bets. Sure, Allar looks like he has the higher ceiling. But so did Robert Griffin III, when Washington drafted two quarterbacks in 2012. Yet, Kirk Cousins is the one still playing in the NFL.
Retaining the most valuable players: If the Steelers keep four quarterbacks, they’ll have to make tough decisions elsewhere. Some players sitting on the fringe who may lose their spot on the 53-man roster include: Backup center Ryan McCollum, defensive linemen Dean Lowry and Esezi Otomewo, an inside linebacker, tight end Robert Tonyan and safety Rayshawn Jenkins. From that group, the Steelers probably have to find four players to cut (that’s already assuming Kaleb Johnson will be cut in favor of Travis Homer). There’s always the risk that another team would sign one of these veterans off the Steelers’ practice squad. But it’s probably a lot easier to find a depth defensive lineman or an interior offensive lineman than it would be to find a quarterback. From a pure asset management standpoint, a quarterback is more valuable (potentially in a trade when it comes to Rudolph, or potentially as the future in the case of the young QBs).
What if they don’t need Rudolph — or worse, he doesn’t win? While I firmly believe Rudolph is the QB most capable of stepping in and keeping the season afloat for a game or two, what if he doesn’t? Last year, Rodgers broke a wrist and the Steelers called on Rudolph. He turned the ball over twice in a loss to the Bears. This entire argument has been under the pretense that the Steelers will need a win — and Rudolph will deliver it. Exactly the right situation needs to unfold to make keeping Rudolph worth it. While he saved the season in 2023 with a three-game winning streak, there’s no guarantee that 1) the Steelers will need a backup for just a game or two (if it’s any longer, they should just look toward the future); 2) the Steelers will still be in playoff position when the injury occurs and 3) Rudolph will deliver.
Would anyone pick up Howard? Howard came into the league as the 185th pick of the 2025 draft. That means he was passed over 184 times. Seven other quarterbacks went ahead of him: Cam Ward, Jaxson Dart, Tyler Shough, Jalen Milroe, Dillon Gabriel, Shedeur Sanders and Kyle McCord. If that’s what the rest of the NFL thought of him in 2025 — how many minds has he changed this preseason, especially after he threw two interceptions against the Jets ? Depending how the final preseason game goes, the Steelers may be able to sneak Howard through to the practice squad.
Is Howard too good to let go? Even if the Steelers believe in McCarthy’s developmental approach, how much better is Howard than other options? He’s a proven winner with resilience , yes. At Ohio State, he picked himself up off the mat after losing in the last game of the 2024 regular season to Michigan and rallied the Buckeyes for a national championship. Still, in terms of arm strength, mobility and other tangible traits, he doesn’t necessarily have one standout quality. While the Steelers like Howard, they have to decide if he’s truly irreplaceable if — and it’s a big if —…

title: Grading Hjalte Froholdt’s New Cardinals Contract: Why Both Sides Win Big
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals put pen to paper today on starting center Hjalte Froholdt's new contract extension, ensuring a core piece of their offensive line is with the team at least through the 2028 season.
Froholdt, previously set for free agency after this season, now remains in the desert for what could be a quicker turnaround than expected under new head coach Mike LaFleur .
When evaluating the deal from all sides, it's tough not to love it.
Perhaps more than anything, Froholdt is a beloved member of the Cardinals' locker room. He consistently is praised for not only his performance on the field, but his leadership and work ethic away from the hashmarks.
Froholdt, initially signing with the Cardinals in 2023 to simply compete for a role along Arizona's offensive line, has transformed into a concrete member of the starting five and hasn't looked back.
His mix of physicality in the interior and football IQ to organize his teammates and set protections before the ball's even snapped was highlighted by LaFleur earlier in camp.
"You can see Fro is tight with all these guys, but I know that those quarterbacks, as we build this thing even more, will appreciate when Fro has the ability to make such changes," said LaFleur.
So, Froholdt's a solid player to have in the locker room and huddle. What about his actual performance?
Froholdt has quietly been one of the league's more underrated centers since emerging as a starter. The best ability is availability, and he's provided just that after starting all 17 games in each of the last three seasons.
On top of that, Froholdt has consistently graded well in advanced metrics, ranking at No. 8 in Pro Football Focus' list of top centers entering the 2026 season.
Top 10 Centers in the NFL Ahead of the 2026 Season🛡️ Save 33% on PFF+ Subscription: https://t.co/U1sKSbMXdq pic.twitter.com/6KpSNl5vB6
Froholdt committed just three penalties last season on 1,121 snaps, two of which were either declined or offset according to Pro Football Reference. He allowed just two quarterback hits and one sack, per Pro Football Focus.
Character? Check . Availability? Check. Proven talent? Check.
But does the money make sense?
For two years and $20 million, it sure does.
Froholdt, who is 30 years old, is a bit of an outlier in terms of starting centers that inked a contract at his age. Only three centers in the top 20 of overall contract value (Froholdt, Elgton Jenkins and Jake Brendel) were 30 years or older at the time of signing.
In terms of overall value, Froholdt's $20 million ranks 13th for his position according to Spotrac.
While exact details have yet to emerge in terms of language, guarantees, etc., Froholdt's $10 million average per season is tied for tenth with Tyler Biadasz.
It's a slight paybump for Froholdt, who inked a two-year and $12 million extension with the Cardinals previously — though the Cardinals also clearly aren't breaking the bank for a generally solid and consistent presence.
Froholdt is now a top-ten center in terms of cash, though the length of the contract also ensures the Cardinals aren't tied to him long-term if his play declines.
This contract, details pending, is very much a win-win for both sides. When grading this deal, it's truly hard to find anything wrong with the contract.

title: Trey Benson Returns to Cardinals, But His 2026 Season in Arizona Is Over
full_text:
ARIZONA — After the Arizona Cardinals waived Trey Benson with an injury designation, the third-year running back cleared waivers and is now back on the team's injured reserve list.
According to the NFL transaction wire, Benson was bypassed by all other 31 teams on the waiver list before landing back in Arizona. Traditionally, other teams will allow a player with a waived/injured designation to clear so they can land on IR in what's generally considered a procedural move.
Benson is working his way back from a meniscus injury that required surgery after he went down in Week 4 of last season.
Since Benson was placed on injured reserve before final roster cuts, he will effectively be out for the entire 2026 season — at least in Arizona. If Benson regains full health, the two sides can reach an injury settlement, which would allow Benson to hit the open market and potentially play elsewhere in 2026.
Benson was not spotted at Cardinals practice in recent days while his early participation was mostly restricted to individual drills during training camp practices. He did not play in any preseason games after a ramp-up to team activities saw a "flare-up" according to Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur.
LaFleur spoke with reporters minutes before Benson was waived with an injury designation:
"We're just taking it one day at a time with Trey right now. Truly, that's all I got for you with that," said LaFleur, who was then asked if Benson would be an injured reserve candidate.
"We'll probably have a better understanding of that, I would say, after we get out of this game."
As fate would have it, the Cardinals officially revealed less than an hour later that Benson would be placed on waivers, effectively ending his 2026 season in Arizona before it even started.
Benson struggled during his first two seasons in the desert after arriving with high expectations as the second running back taken in his class. His ability to break-off big runs at Florida State was only spotted irregularly with the Cardinals.
As for Arizona's running back room moving forward, the Cardinals will rely on a heavy 1-2 punch of Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier while James Conner is poised to take on RB3 duties.
Bam Knight also figures to be a strong rotational back with high chances of making the roster following his exclusion with starters in last week's preseason game.

title: Cardinals Excited to Join 'Special' Packers Training Camp Tradition
full_text:
ARIZONA — Life, oftentimes, is like riding a bike.
Sometimes you just need to get out of the scorching desert heat to do it.
The Arizona Cardinals pack their bags for their preseason finale against the Green Bay Packers with a joint practice scheduled for Wednesday and the actual game set for Friday. Starters are unlikely to play in the finale, placing a special emphasis on their practice with Green Bay — for a few reasons.
The Cardinals will take part in the beloved tradition of riding bikes with kids to practice, a two-wheeled heritage that initially dates back to the late 1950s, where children would line up outside of the Packers' locker room to offer rides to the practice field.
It's one of the league's most recognizable events, and Arizona's excited to take part.
"It's a cool place. They got the bikes with the kids and stuff like that, and that's for a cool cause for the locals. And so we'll do that too, just like a lot of the other teams do when they joint [practice]," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said during his Monday press conference.
LaFleur is also set to face his brother and Packers head coach Matt LaFleur. The only other active brother/head coach duo in the NFL is Jim and John Harbaugh.
"You got to be on the same page, so it's easier, I would say, to be on the same page with your brother who you talk to about five times a day anyway. So that's been really good," LaFleur added on facing up against his brother.
The Packers have already put out a request for young fans of any team to bring their bikes prior to practice so the Cardinals can also participate in the tradition.
Cardinals defensive lineman Roy Lopez was pretty amped to enjoy the bicycle ride — even if the Packers fans might not know exactly who he is.
"It's cool, man. Because you see the pictures, it's their tradition over there. So it's awesome, man. Any sort of way you can share a smile with somebody that's just there for the love of the game, and they don't even necessarily need to know who you are, right? It's just for the love of football, man," Lopez said.
"For the love of just being able to share those whatever 5, 10 minutes and share that memory, it's heartwarming. It's a good way to start practice or finish practice. I don't know when we do it, but it keeps you going, man. It's something that I know my family or my lady's gonna ask about, 'How was that?' So it's gonna be really cool."

title: Cardinals Reach Contract Extension With Key Offensive Starter
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are set to keep Hjalte Froholdt around.
The Cardinals reportedly reached a two-year contract extension with their starting center worth $20 million, according to NFL Media's Ian Rapoport.
Sources: The #AZCardinals and C Hjalte Froholdt have agreed to terms on a 2-year, $20M contract extension, keeping him in the fold through the 2028 season. One of their most consistent performances and anchors of their O-lines gets rewarded. pic.twitter.com/k8u0jI7CJe
It's a well deserved deal for Froholdt, who has anchored the Cardinals' offensive line for multiple years now and has truly grown into a key part of Arizona's starting unit. He's started all 51 games played in the desert and has largely provided availability and high level of play.
"Personally you always got to get your own mindset ready for all the physical things going to happen. It's also a little bit of mental. There's all the stuff like okay, how am I doing? How's practice going? Am I the same as I am last year? What are we doing? Yada yada. But I think one thing I've just learned is just stick to the simple things," Froholdt said at the beginning of training camp.
"So I'm back. I'm playing the game that I love. I get to share cool experiences with a lot of a lot of pretty awesome people, and I get to play as a Cardinal. So I'm pretty stoked about that. So yeah,it  feels really good."
Froholdt, who was initially set to be a free agent at the end of the season, now gets a well-deserved payraise and will provide continuity for a Cardinals line that also has Paris Johnson Jr. and Isaac Seumalo under contract through the 2027 season.
Froholdt, despite his high level of play, is barely recognized in a national spotlight. Perhaps that can change with more offensive success driven by first-year head coach Mike LaFleur, who has impressed Froholdt.
"I think it's fun having LaFleur out there. He's kind of like a crazy offensive coordinator mentality, like he goes in, stops everything, and just starts teaching. It's so fun to have that," Froholdt said.
"He's a head coach, but an offensive-minded head coach coming in and he loves these teaching moments. Yeah, we might get a break, or well, we're not going to get all the reps in, or whatever. But he's in it, because then everybody listens, and I think it's awesome to understand that.
"Like a receiver needs to understand why we're blocking certain ways. Not that I necessarily know routes, but I need to understand what type — like is it a deeper throw concept, or what's entailed in the protections? We're really all encompassing. So that's been really fun so far."
Froholdt's been one of few steady and consistent players in the Cardinals' lineup through the last few seasons. It's nice to see him rewarded.

title: Injuries Force Cardinals to Make 2 Roster Moves Ahead of Packers Game
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals move into their preseason finale against the Green Bay Packers with a few notable injuries to keep tabs on.
Arizona will be without punter Blake Gillikin this week thanks to a groin injury suffered during pre-game warm-ups last week vs. Dallas while safety Dadrion Taylor-Demerson left action after a big hit with a Cowboys receiver.
As a result, the Cardinals brought some reinforcements into the building as they pack their bags for Wisconsin.
Arizona officially signed punterJack Browning and safety Josh Minkins.
More on both from the team's media relations department:
"Browning (5-11, 190) played for the Orlando Storm of the UFL where he appeared in 11 games and punted 29 times for 1,408 yards (48.5 avg.), landing 11 punts inside the 20-yard line. He originally entered the NFL as an undrafted rookie free agent with Buffalo in 2024 out of San Diego State and spent time with the Bills and Ravens during the offseason before signing with Tampa Bay's practice squad. Browning appeared in five games with the Buccaneers in 2024 and punted 10 times for 425 yards (42.5 avg.)."
"Minkins (6-1, 207) also most recently played with the Orlando Storm of the UFL where he appeared in seven games and tallied 32 tackles (22 solo), three passes defensed and one fumble recovery. He entered the NFL in 2025 with New England as an undrafted rookie free agent from Cincinnati. In his five-year collegiate career at Cincinnati (2024) and Louisville (2020-23), Minkins played 51 games (28 starts) and posted 144 tackles (96 solo), 3.5 tackles for loss, one sack,18 passes defensed, four interceptions, one forced fumble and a fumble recovery."
The Cardinals will wrap up their preseason in Green Bay on Friday, marking the final of four exhibition games before their regular season begins. Arizona is unlikely to play their starters thanks to a joint practice beforehand on Wednesday.
"For the most part, I think they like it because again, they get to go against someone else," LaFleur said of the joint practice.
"Like I think our receivers are getting sick of running the same routes over and over and over versus our corners. We don't want it to just turn into a double move fest every single day in practice just to try to win practice. We want to get sharpened at the stuff that we're going to do more than we're not. So from that standpoint, it ends up being good."

title: Key Cardinals Missing From Monday Practice
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals returned to Tempe for their first and only home practice of the week before packing their bags for a trip to Green Bay.
Missing were some notable names including James Conner, Jeremiyah Love, Isaiah Adams and Isaac Seumalo today.
It's plausible most, if not all, were simply veteran rest days — though the team has a scheduled travel day tomorrow before their joint practice with the Packers.
Arizona, with their starting two offensive guards out of the lineup, rolled out Hayden Conner and Jon Gaines with their offensive line.
I do not see Isaiah Adams or Isaac Seumalo here at Cardinals practice. Jon Gaines was at right guard while Hayden Conner was at left guard with the first team offense. No James Conner or Jeremiyah Love here. pic.twitter.com/SU7VnUbHDP
Conner has been a hit-and-miss participant in practice lately, as the veteran running back is either looking to preserve his health for the regular season or is still managing a foot/ankle injury suffered in Week 3 of last season.
Previously speaking with reporters, head coach Mike LaFleur says Conner has earned the right to decide if he'll play in preseason — which hasn't been the case thus far. Green Bay is Arizona's final exhibition matchup ahead of the regular season.
Trey Benson was also not present — he was actually waived today. You can read more about that here .
Love continues to rest from a reported high ankle sprain suffered two games ago in Las Vegas, one that hasn't seen him practice in just under two weeks.
"He's doing well, progressing well, and kind of in the next phase of it," LaFleur said of Love today. He also added Love wouldn't be practicing, which isn't a surprise.
Seumalo has sometimes gotten veteran rest days in camp, so his absence isn't completely surprising. The free agent signing has been a consistent presence in prior stops at Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, so Arizona likely wants to keep him fresh and ready for their season opener.
Adams' absence is likely the most eye-opening, as the third-year guard isn't quite there in terms of earning those days off — especially with this being his first year as a full-time starter with inconsistent play in the prior two seasons.
Star pass rusher Josh Sweat did indeed return today from the PUP list — you can check that out here .
The Cardinals are unlikely to play their starters in Friday's preseason battle in Green Bay, mostly thanks to Wednesday's joint practice against the Packers. With Arizona traveling on Tuesday, we likely won't find out if any of the absences are serious until later in the week.

title: 3 Big Reasons Why the Cardinals Finally Gave Up on Trey Benson
full_text:
ARIZONA — They finally did it.
It was a day many saw coming in the Arizona Cardinals' facility as running back Trey Benson was officially waived/injured by the team in a flurry of roster moves announced Monday that also included Josh Sweat's return.
Benson, entering his third season, has mostly been sidelined due to a meniscus injury suffered last season. He was thought to be recovered entering training camp, though that clearly wasn't the case.
Now, the Day 2 pick moves on elsewhere while the Cardinals officially wipe their hands clean of the Florida State product.
X brutally honest takeaways from the move:
The Cardinals saw Benson exit with his knee injury in Week 4 of last season and he hasn't quite been the same since. Initially Arizona opened his practice window after he made a recovery from knee surgery to return late in 2025 before ultimately placing him on season-ending injured reserve.
After months of rehab, Benson was expected to return to training camp fresh and ready to fight for a roster spot. Benson initially participated in individual drills, though when he was finally upgraded to team activities, Benson's knee couldn't cooperate after suffering a "flare-up" with preseason play practically eliminated.
Benson, towards the end of his tenure, wasn't spotted practicing with the Cardinals — and it's a shame he hasn't been healthy for nearly a full year now.
Benson needed to have a strong camp/preseason to make the roster, though Bam Knight's emergence might have just been the difference between Benson hitting PUP/IR and him flat-out being waived like he was today.
One question the Cardinals find themselves heavily debating is how many running backs they'll ultimately keep on the final roster — and if that number is indeed four, Knight clearly has that final spot taken.
That's partly due to simply his availability, though Knight also emerged as a special teams contributor and strong rotational running back when called upon.
Perhaps if the Cardinals didn't have an obvious alternative, more time/patience would have been bought for Benson. However, Knight's performance made the decision easy for Arizona.
The Cardinals would have desperately loved to get something in return for Benson before ultimately cutting him, though the trade market around him was practically non-existent for a few reasons.
It's tough to get something of value when teams are anticipating getting Benson available on the waiver wire. Why give up draft capital if you could possibly get him for free?
His injury also muddied those waters. Potential inquiring teams probably wanted to see Benson healthy and on the field before making a move, though his flare-up ultimately may have cost the Cardinals.
It's not as if Benson's prior body of work was enough to warrant a return, either. Besides a handful of big runs, he was largely inconsistent as an NFL running back.
Perhaps that can change elsewhere, though Benson's time in the desert was clearly done.
