title: Colts Reveal New ‘Anvil Strike’ Rivalries Uniform
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts finally have the dark uniform combo this fanbase has been begging for.
Indianapolis unveiled its new “Anvil Strike” Nike Rivalries uniform Tuesday, giving the Colts a completely different look built around a dark anthracite jersey, metallic blue helmet and silver accents. The uniform will make its debut Sept. 27 against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium.
more than a gameday tradition. pic.twitter.com/xoUrYZXsUn
The Colts have one of the cleanest and most recognizable uniforms in football, but there is only so much you can do with blue and white.
The Indiana Nights alternate gave Indianapolis something different, but this is the dark look the Colts have desperately needed for a long time. Nike calls the color “Anvil Steel,” with the design inspired by the pregame anvil tradition at Lucas Oil Stadium.
The jersey is dark without trying too hard to turn the Colts into something they are not. Classic speed blue numbers, reflective finishes and the traditional shoulder stripes keep enough of the classic identity while still making the uniform feel completely different.
The Colts describe the anvil as a symbol of strength, resilience and the relentless spirit of the franchise, and that inspiration carries throughout the entire uniform.
It is dark, aggressive and still looks like the Colts.
the official lineup. pic.twitter.com/kTqOkGwKs9
What makes the uniform stand out, though, is how much detail Indianapolis worked into the design.
For the first time in franchise history, the horseshoe is actually integrated into the jersey itself, with a silver metallic version appearing on the shoulders. The traditional shoulder stripes have also been updated alongside horseshoe-inspired grommets.
Reflective accents throughout the uniform are designed to represent the sparks created when the anvil is struck.
“For The Shoe” is printed inside the collar as a tribute to Colts fans, while “INDY” appears on the front helmet bumper as a nod to Indianapolis.
The metallic blue helmet will probably generate the most conversation, simply because it is such a drastic change from the traditional white shell. But paired with the dark jersey and silver details, it fits the overall look.
okay, another look at the helmet. 👀 pic.twitter.com/9vfUhl0Bdz
Indianapolis has always leaned heavily into tradition when it comes to its uniforms, and there is nothing wrong with that. The blue and white combination is one of the cleanest looks in the league.
The Colts did not need a complete redesign; they just needed an alternate that actually felt different.
Anvil Strike accomplishes that without completely abandoning what makes a Colts uniform recognizable.
The Rivalries program will have every AFC South team wearing a special uniform in 2026, with each club wearing its set once per season through 2028.
For the Colts, their first shot comes against Houston in Week 3.
And when they finally hit the field at Lucas Oil Stadium, the new uniforms should make a statement.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts' Brian Mason Provides Latest Update on Kicking Battle
full_text:
Of all the Indianapolis Colts position battles we have watched unfold throughout training camp, the most interesting competition has been at a position you might not expect: Kicker.
The Colts have witnessed Blake Grupe and Spencer Shrader each state their case for who should be Indy's kicker in 2026. Both have shown why the Colts believe they have two starting kickers on the roster, making the decision even harder.
After the first couple of weeks of camp, Grupe seemed to be running away with the job . However, the momentum shifted to Shrader over the second half of training camp, and the competition seems to be up for grabs yet again.
"As a whole, as we look at everything through pre-practice, live kicks in games, Grupe's kicking at 86 percent. Shrader's kicking at 81 percent,"  special teams coordinator Brian Mason explained. "Grupe had a really strong first two weeks, which we've all kind of talked about in live kicks and in practice. Shrader really closed the gap, I think, these last two weeks."
Grupe started training camp on fire, going multiple practices in front of the media without missing a kick. He backed up what he put on the field last season when he went a perfect 11-of-11 after joining the Colts.
But Grupe's recent preseason performances have warranted concern. Grupe is 0-of-2 through two contests, including a missed 36-yard attempt that would normally be a chip shot. While he has been steady throughout the summer, Grupe needs to make his kicks in game situations.
"I think Grupe has been really consistent throughout all of training camp," Mason stated. "Obviously, he had an unfortunate miss that is uncharacteristic to him in the game, and we know that he's kicked at a really high level both in games and in practice for us."
Shrader's journey this summer has been the opposite of Grupe's. Working his way back from a torn ACL and MCL, Shrader started off camp with shaky performances, pushing his kicks to the left. At one point, Shrader was only making 69% of his field goal attempts.
However, Shrader has been steadily improving as training camp has progressed. The accuracy issues have subsided, and he is striking the ball very well. Shrader is 4-of-4 in the preseason , including makes of 53 and 61 yards.
"We knew that it wasn't going to be smooth for (Shrader) to start training camp," Mason admitted. "I think you saw him make some improvements. I think he really finished the week strong in joint practice against the Falcons. He had two opportunities to have two-minute kicks, which he hit both true right down the middle. Did a really good job with that. Obviously, he made his two kicks within the game."
While Grupe still holds the edge in overall percentage, it's quite feasible to believe that Shrader has the edge in the competition . Mason previously stated that the kicks in live situations would mean more when determining who will be the Colts' kicker this season. Shrader has been far superior in this category so far, and Mason echoed his earlier thoughts on in-game kicks.
“In-game kicks carry the most weight," Mason said. "So, I don't have a formula that's sitting here with a magic answer. We have two really good kickers, and it's really – like we said two weeks ago, hey, we're not going to judge somebody on one day or judge somebody in the first two weeks. We're going to see how do they progress through training camp, and who do we believe can be the best starting kicker for us for 17 regular season games, and then hopefully into the playoffs."
The Colts must trim their roster to 53 players by 6 p.m. ET on Sunday. That gives both kickers one week to make their final push for the job. Both will receive plenty of reps this week to prove it, and one more preseason game against the Detroit Lions to show they can be the guy.
"We have a really good situation to be in, where I think we have two talented kickers," Mason remarked. "Shrader's starting to kick to the ability level that we kind of expect him to be able to kick at. Grupe's been really consistent throughout training camp.
"We're going to put pressure on those guys and kick a little bit more this week than we would in a normal game week, and obviously we'll still split their reps in the game, which will be determined based on how they kick throughout the week in practice on Tuesday and Thursday."
If the decision had to be made today, Shrader would be the likely pick. Luckily for Grupe, there is still time to show he can overcome his recent struggles.
The result of Saturday's game will not matter, but how these two kickers perform certainly will.

title: Colts Fantasy Football Sleepers to Target in 2026
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts could quietly be one of the best teams to target for fantasy football value this season.
Jonathan Taylor is already an established fantasy superstar, but Daniel Jones, Tyler Warren, Josh Downs, Alec Pierce and now Keenan Allen all have a chance to outperform their current draft position if Indianapolis’ offense stays healthy.
First up, and this should come as no surprise to anyone following the Colts: RB Jonathan Taylor.
Taylor led the NFL in carries (323), total touchdowns (20) and rushing touchdowns (18) last season while finishing third with 1,585 rushing yards. ESPN currently has his consensus ADP at No. 7 overall.
But don’t overthink it. JT remains one of the safest bets for elite fantasy volume.
This is where the Colts start to get interesting from a value standpoint.
Daniel Jones is going around QB24 in consensus ADP despite ranking QB5 in fantasy scoring through the first 10 weeks of 2025 before injuries derailed his season. He threw 15 touchdowns and added five more on the ground during that stretch.
The Achilles is the obvious concern, but Jones has been full-go in camp. As long as he stays healthy, his dual-threat ability in Shane Steichen’s offense gives him legitimate top-10 upside at a late-round price.
Warren finished his rookie season with 76 catches for 817 yards and four receiving touchdowns, plus another score on the ground, finishing as TE5 in fantasy.
He is already being drafted as TE4, and even with another proven target now joining the offense, Warren should remain one of Jones’ most important weapons.
Warren may not be a massive steal, but he has a real chance to outperform that price.
The addition of Keenan Allen changes things for this Colts receiving corps .
Allen caught 81 passes for 777 yards and four touchdowns on 122 targets with the Los Angeles Chargers last season. Now reunited with Steichen, he is probably the best candidate to absorb a large portion of the 111 targets left behind by Michael Pittman Jr.
At 34 years old, big-play upside isn’t exactly the reason to draft Allen. But his ability to get open underneath and consistently earn targets makes him an interesting late-round option, especially in PPR leagues.
Pierce’s injury could actually create some value in fantasy drafts.
He finished last season with 1,003 yards and six touchdowns while leading the NFL with 21.3 yards per reception. Even if it takes a few weeks for him to get back to full speed, Pierce is one of the league’s best deep threats when healthy.
If the injury pushes his ADP down far enough, he is absolutely worth taking a chance on later in the draft.
This is my favorite value play of the group.
Downs is entering the final year of his rookie contract and sits around WR42 in PPR ADP after catching 58 passes for 566 yards and four touchdowns last season. He will have plenty of opportunity, and Downs has already acknowledged there should be more opportunities for him this season.
Bottom line: Jonathan Taylor is still the guy, and Tyler Warren will remain one of the best tight ends in fantasy football.
But if you are looking for Colts players who could help win you a league without costing an early pick, Daniel Jones and Josh Downs remain two of my favorite values, while Keenan Allen and Alec Pierce are both worth taking a chance on if they fall far enough.

title: One Concern That Hasn't Been Solved Yet (And How Colts Can Fix It)
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have a much better idea of how their 2026 regular season roster will look after wrapping up training camp late last week , but there are still numerous spots on the depth chart that need convincing.
Head coach Shane Steichen has a training camp and two preseason games to pull from, and while most of the preseason's position battles have a clear favorite, some have brought more questions than answers .
The Colts have their starting center for the foreseeable future in Tanor Bortolini, a budding star in his own right , but what lies beneath him is uninspiring.
Quality offensive line depth is so hard to come by in the NFL that it could be considered oxymoronic.
Teams rarely have five quality starters across the offensive front, and those who do greedily strive to field a reliable swing option or two.
The Indianapolis Colts have been fortunate to have top-tier starting units throughout the Chris Ballard era and, more recently, have had solid reserve options on standby, but this year looks bleak .
Offensive line coach Tony Sparano Jr.'s projected reserve unit features two intriguing options in rookie guard Jalen Farmer and tackle Luke Tenuta. Still, neither is quite spot-start ready just yet.
The biggest concern across the second-team offense's trenches resides at the center of it all.
The Colts lost longtime backup center Danny Pinter in free agency earlier this offseason when he signed with the Baltimore Ravens to compete for a starting job, and they've been feeling this loss ever since.
Shane Steichen, Tony Sparano Jr., and Co. elected to move third-year guard Dalton Tucker inside to be Pinter's replacement, but the experience throughout training camp and now preseason play has been worrisome.
Tucker struggled to find consistency with either of the Colts' reserve quarterbacks from the start of camp to the finish, resulting in constant snap mishaps that would ultimately derail the corresponding 11-on-11 session.
And now, two preseason games into the 2026 season and Tucker continues to struggle. He had numerous plays during the Colts' 34-6 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Saturday that ended the play before it could begin.
“I thought he's done a nice job. Obviously, it's a new spot for him and a new role and there's a lot on the center's plate," head coach Shane Steichen said about Tucker's transition inside thus far.
"But I think he's taken it really well mentally and he's still working through that process. But I like his physicality there at that spot. Obviously, rotating from guard to there, that's a big transition, but I thought he's handled it well.”
The transition to a new position is no doubt commendable, but Tucker feels destined to kick back out while the Colts are forced to look for a backup center elsewhere.
The Colts could very well trade for a veteran center for backup duties, but they're more likely to wait for cut day to address their situation before giving up draft capital.
General manager Chris Ballard is likely already scouring the projected waiver wire market, so be on the lookout for a potential claim across the interior offensive line.

title: Colts Report Card: Depth Struggles in Blowout Loss to Falcons
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts rested most of their starters against the Atlanta Falcons on Saturday, and their backups gave them very little reason to feel comfortable about the depth behind them.
Indianapolis was dominated 34-6, outgained 461 yards to 164 and failed to score a touchdown. From an offense that could barely move the ball to a defense that made Atlanta UDFA QB Jack Strand look like a Hall of Famer, there were not many positives to take away.
Here is how each Colts position group graded after Saturday’s loss.
Anthony Richardson still looks like the favorite over Riley Leonard in the battle to back up Daniel Jones, but neither quarterback gave Indianapolis much on Saturday.
Leonard finished 7-of-14 for 62 yards, while Richardson went 3-of-9 for 24 yards. Combined, the two completed just 43.5% of their passes for 86 yards with zero touchdowns.
The offensive line certainly did them no favors, but neither quarterback consistently elevated the offense around him. Indianapolis scored only six points, went 1-of-11 on third down and never found the end zone.
The Colts rested their starting offensive line, giving several depth pieces an opportunity to make their case for roster spots. Not many took advantage.
Indianapolis struggled to create consistent running lanes and allowed Richardson to be sacked twice in the second half. A penalty on center Josh Kreutz also wiped away one of Richardson’s better completions.
The quarterbacks were under pressure too often, and the unit never gave the offense a chance to establish any sort of rhythm.
It is difficult for a receiver room to make much noise when the entire offense finishes with 86 passing yards, but this group did little to help change that.
Coleman Owen provided essentially the only explosive play through the air with a 39-yard reception. Deion Burks caught four passes for 19 yards, while D.J. Montgomery, Eli Pancol and Pharaoh Brown combined for only 23 yards.
With several receivers still competing for the final roster spots, Saturday was a missed opportunity for somebody to separate himself.
Atlanta controlled the line of scrimmage for most of the afternoon, rushing for 164 yards while their quarterbacks operated comfortably in the pocket.
UDFA DT Cameron Ball recorded a sack, and players like DT Tim Smith and rookie DE George Gumbs Jr. flashed on individual snaps, but there was never consistent disruption.
When Indianapolis did begin collapsing the pocket, Atlanta's quarterbacks repeatedly scrambled and extended plays. For a unit facing mostly reserves, the lack of consistent disruption was concerning.
The linebackers were probably the most average position group on the field.
Austin Ajiake and Jaylon Carlies tied for the team lead with six tackles, while Bryce Boettcher recorded four tackles and a tackle for loss. Rookie CJ Allen also made his preseason debut and finished with three tackles in limited action.
The impact plays were not there. Atlanta consistently sustained drives, and nobody from this group did enough to change the direction of the game.
Either Minnesota State UDFA QB Jack Strand is elite or the Colts' secondary depth has some serious work to do.
Strand completed 12-of-17 passes for 212 yards and a touchdown, while Cooper Rush went 10-of-11 for 86 yards. Atlanta finished with 297 net passing yards and consistently found openings throughout the Indianapolis secondary.
Cam Taylor-Britt and Jaylon Jones each made nice plays in coverage, but those moments were overwhelmed by everything else. The Falcons drove the field almost whenever they wanted, and Indianapolis never forced a turnover.
There is only so much stock to put into a preseason game without most of the starters, but Saturday showed just how much work is left to be done.
The Colts did not just lose. Their depth got dominated in nearly every facet of the game.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts' Position Battle Updates Following Brutal Falcons Loss
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts had a Saturday they'd soon like to forget after falling to the Atlanta Falcons 34-6. Mistakes were prevalent on all sides of the ball, leaving the Colts with plenty to clean up before they finish the preseason next weekend.
Despite the embarrassing loss, there were new developments at multiple positions. Here are the latest updates on the position battles across the Colts' roster.
After Anthony Richardson Sr. had a solid performance against the New England Patriots last week, the backup quarterback competition between Richardson and Riley Leonard looked closer than it has ever been. Unfortunately, neither quarterback helped themselves on Saturday.
Leonard got the start and finished 7-of-14 (50%) for 62 yards in the first half, struggling to move the ball and throw under pressure. Richardson did not fare well either, going 3-of-9 (33%) for 24 passing yards and 15 rushing yards.
The struggles of Leonard and Richardson should definitely give Colts' fans pause about the backup quarterback position. Richardson has looked better as of late, but the competition is still neck and neck heading into the final week of the preseason.
DJ Giddens has not yet returned from a hamstring injury he suffered in camp, paving the way for rookie Seth McGowan to seize the RB2 role. While McGowan had only 27 yards on eight carries Saturday, he continued to show his powerful running style and ability to get yards after initial contact.
The Colts' coaching staff loves what they have seen from McGowan in camp, and the rookie has received plenty of reps with the first-team offense as well. The backup running back role is McGowan's to lose at this point, and the Colts may finally have a back that can give Jonathan Taylor some much-needed breaks throughout the season.
With the Colts signing Keenan Allen last Monday, most of the wide receiver room is set. However, there is likely one more spot available between a group that includes Laquon Treadwell, Coleman Owen, and Deion Burks.
It was Burks who helped his case the most against the Falcons. The rookie hauled in four catches for 19 yards and averaged 24 yards per kick return. Burks has been seeing more action as of late and is beginning to take advantage of his opportunities.
Even though Burks was more involved, Owen may be the wide receiver who ends up with the roster spot. He hauled in a 39-yard catch of his own from Leonard and is currently the Colts' starting return man. Burks has been closing the gap, but Owen's special teams prowess may end up getting him the spot on cutdown day.
As expected, the Colts continued to rotate their linebacker group on Saturday. With Akeem Davis-Gaither resting, the starting linebackers were veterans Jaylon Carlies and Austin Ajiake. Second-round rookie CJ Allen and fourth-round rookie Bryce Boettcher rotated in on the next series as the Colts gave each player plenty of reps throughout the game.
Carlies (six tackles) continues to trend upward , playing a majority of the reps with the first-team defense in practice, and was one of the only Colts to make plays against the Falcons. Allen (three tackles) had a few nice reps during the game but struggled to get off blocks at times.
Allen was seen as the presumed starter at MIKE when the Colts began training camp. However, Allen missing practice due to injuries, combined with Carlies' strong play, has made this position battle much more interesting than many imagined. While the Colts are still expected to rotate their linebackers, it could be Carlies who receives the lion's share of the snaps.
The Colts are set at their first four cornerback spots. Behind that is anyone's guess, as the depth cornerbacks continued to struggle.
Mehki Blackmon was a liability in coverage yet again, drawing another defensive pass interference penalty. Rob Carter Jr. was given the start next to Blackmon, but he did not fare much better in coverage, especially when guarding the flat. Johnathan Edwards had trouble locating the football when it was thrown his way, leading to multiple catches.
The best cornerback out of the group looked to be Jaylon Jones. While Jones made a few plays in coverage, it seems Lou Anarumo still does not believe Jones is a fit for his defense, considering the fourth-year player remained in the game late in the fourth quarter.
The depth at cornerback is in rough shape for the Colts. Do not be surprised if cornerback is a position the Colts target heavily when cuts happen around the league.
Before Saturday's game, it looked like Blake Grupe had all but sealed the kicker competition over Spencer Shrader. Grupe has been kicking around 90% in practices open to the media, while Shrader has only connected on 69% of his kicks.
But when the bright lights of the game come on, Shrader has been the better of the two. He knocked in two more field goals on Saturday as Grupe missed his lone attempt. Shrader is now 4-of-4 on field goals in game action while Grupe is 0-of-2, a stark contrast to practice.
Kicks made during a game obviously hold much more weight than kicks made in practice. For that reason, Shrader has made this a battle again and could be on the verge of winning the competition entirely.

title: 4 Winners, 3 Losers From Colts' Loss to Falcons: Rookie WR Stands Out
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts had little to write home about in their 34-6 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Saturday, but a handful of players did positively stand out.
The Colts had more losers than they did winners, with position groups as a whole being questioned throughout , so instead of touching on each individual who had an uninspired performance, we're narrowing it down to the team's three biggest losers.
Follow along as I break down each winner and loser of the Colts' brutal preseason loss against the Atlanta Falcons.
The Colts could have an all-star starting cornerback in Sauce Gardner, Charvarius Ward Sr., and Justin Walley, but don't sleep on Cam Taylor-Britt.
Taylor-Britt exited training camp as the de facto CB4 who can slide in at nickel or boundary cornerback if called up, and only continued that upward trajectory during the Colts' preseason loss to the Falcons.
He had four tackles (three solo) against Atlanta on Saturday, and his impressive run fits and sticky coverage looked exactly like each of the practices at Grand Park over the past few weeks of training camp.
Lou Anarumo welcomed Taylor-Britt back to defense after their years together with the Cincinnati Bengals, and it appears that
The Colts' kicking competition between veterans Blake Grupe and Spencer Shrader has taken a wildly interesting turn.
Grupe exited training camp as the clear favorite to win the team's starting placekicker job after he made 90% of his practice kicks, and Shrader just barely eclipsed a 70% rate.
It's felt like Grupe's job to lose, and after two preseason games, that reality may be setting in.
Spencer Shrader is now 4-for-4 on field goal attempts through two preseason games after going 2-for-2 with a long of 53 yards in the Colts' loss to the Falcons. On the other hand, Grupe missed a 36-yard attempt in the same game and now falls to 0-for-2 on such kicks during preseason play.
It'll be fascinating to see how STC Brian Mason decides to judge their overall performances, because Shrader's ability on gamedays may just give him the edge after all.
The Colts' last pick (7th-round, 254th overall) of the 2026 NFL Draft, wide receiver Deion Burks, had an intriguing showing against the Atlanta Falcons.
Burks was viewed as a potential draft steal early on, but had been quiet throughout training camp. With Alec Pierce's extended absence opening the door for the Colts' wide receiver room, the hope was that Burks would shine brightly in an otherwise dark situation, but even with increased usage, he struggled to prove himself.
Against the Falcons, Burks had just four receptions for 19 receiving yards, but proved to be a reliable option regardless. There were also two penalties by teammates that hurt Burks' day: an offensive penalty that wiped out a strong first-down reception, and one on special teams that took back a strong kick return.
Burks didn't have an all-time statistical performance that suggests he's a lock for the team's final roster spot at wide receiver, but he still showed the biggest increase in stock of anyone on the roster.
Injuries and a new defensive scheme have prevented third-year linebacker Jaylon Carlies from establishing himself as a starting NFL linebacker, but so far throughout the preseason, and specifically as of recently, he's come along nicely.
Carlies exited Colts training camp on a high note , with consecutive practices as the defense's starting linebacker suggesting that an unforeseen emergence could be in order.
He had stacked strong practice performances throughout the last week of training camp, and particularly during the Colts' two-day joint practice with the Falcons , and looked to be a leader for the defense's opening at starting linebacker .
Carlies continued his newfound consistency on Saturday against the Falcons, leading the team with six tackles (five solo). Rookies CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher have had moments of their own throughout training camp, but recently, it seems like Jaylon Carlies is earning a starting spot before our eyes.
The Colts have been betting on second-year defensive end Jaylahn Tuimoloau to take a massive step forward to earn the starting role opposite budding star Laiatu Latu.
Although Tuimoloau shined early in training camp, he has since been a mainstay reserve option. Veteran Arden Key has all but shored up the starting spot in question, and that's hardly due to his positive play, but rather because Tuimoloau has done nothing to suggest he's worth betting on as a first-time, full-time starter in his second season.
Tuimoloau has shown little to nothing in pass rush against backup pass protectors through two games of preseason play thus far, but it's his poor showing in run defense that is most concerning.
The Colts traded a 6th-round pick for cornerback Mekhi Blackmon during last year's preseason to bolster their cornerback room.
Blackmon started in eleven games for the Lou Anarumo's Colts defense in 2025 and had some promising moments throughout, but it's been a completely different story through two preseason games ahead of the 2026 regular season.
Blackmon had two coverage infractions against the New England Patriots in the team's preseason opener, and that continued in Saturday's game against the Atlanta Falcons.
He's clearly in his head at this stage of the preseason, which is bad for any professional athlete, but especially for an NFL cornerback. Teams are targeting him early and often through two preseason games, and such poor play begs the question: Will Mekhi Blackmon make the initial 53-man roster?
Colts' second-year quarterback Riley Leonard has been neck and neck with Anthony Richardson throughout the summer as they battle for the QB2 role behind Daniel Jones, but the two preseason games so far suggest that he's losing ground.
Richardson clearly outshined Leonard during the Colts' preseason opener against the New England Patriots last week, but this week was much different given that both quarterbacks struggled behind an atrocious offensive line.
Neither Leonard nor Richardson had a statistically promising showing against the Atlanta Falcons on Saturday, but the former especially struggled.
Leonard went 7-for-14 for 62 passing yards during his first-half run with the Colts' second-team offense, and for the most part looked lost against the Falcons.
He was given an opportunity to bounce back in a big way this week, but another lackluster showing suggests that he's slipping out of favor in the Colts' QB2 decision.

title: Biggest Takeaways From Colts Preseason Loss to Falcons: Depth Gets Questioned
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts were routed by the Atlanta Falcons 34-6 in their preseason matchup on Saturday.
It was the sloppiest, flattest performance of the preseason, and it has made me question whether their depth can hang if called upon during regular-season play in 2026.
The good news is that the Colts dominated the Falcons during their two-day joint practice at Grand Park earlier this week, which means their starting units definitely have some promise brewing for Week 1's arrival on September 13. However, if the Colts want to make any semblance of noise in the playoffs, their immediate depth will need to step up, and today's showing suggested otherwise.
Follow along as I break down my biggest takeaways from the Colts' uninspired preseason performance against the Falcons.
The Falcons were in complete control of today's game, totaling 461 yards of offense compared to Indy's 164. Lou Anarumo's defense isn't responsible for the offense's lack of production, but it didn't make matters easier.
Atlanta was 9-for-17 on third downs and averaged 6.7 yards per play against the Colts. Falcons QBs Cooper Rush and Jack Strand went a combined 22-28 for 297 passing yards, 1 passing touchdown, and 1 sack through the air.
The Colts entered the summer with a ton of unproven players at linebacker, but have since churned out a solid room from top to bottom. Rookie Bryce Boettcher and veteran Jaylon Carlies had some promising moments in Saturday's bout against the Falcons, and while the linebacker room as a whole didn't have many highlights, if any, they weren't the main reason for the defense's poor performance.
Lou Anarumo's second-team pass rush and secondary combined for a brutal day overall. Veterans CB Cam Taylor-Britt and DT Colby Wooden proved to be the strong backup options they've shown to be throughout training camp, but everyone else's performance said the opposite.
Second-year DE Jaylahn Tuimoloau and veteran CB Mekhi Balckmon were the biggest examples of this, as Saturday's showing made for back-to-back uninspired preseason performances.
The Colts have a ton to iron out before the regular season arrives, and determining the pecking order for their defensive depth chart now feels like a top priority.
The Indianapolis Colts’ backup offensive line largely featured the same unit from start to finish against the Falcons on Saturday, and their uninspired showing reaffirms how dire things look outside of their starting five.
No Jalen Farmer or Luke Tenuta played a role in such negative play, and quarterbacks Riley Leonard and Anthony Richardson struggled as a result. The pair of offensive signal callers had some lowlights on their own, but it was mainly the line’s poor play that caused such dysfunction.
Quality backup linemen are hard to come by in the NFL, but the Colts have been one of those teams in recent years with at least a couple of viable options available. Farmer and Tenuta have flashed as solid options, but outside of them, Indy is left praying that each of their starting five will start in all 17 games in 2026.
The Colts' kicking battle throughout training camp has become Blake Grupe's job to lose , and after two preseason games, Spencer Shrader has rebounded, making it an impossible decision.
Grupe has nailed 90% of kicks during training camp, while Shrader has barely eclipsed the 70% mark, but the preseason showings suggest the opposite trajectory.
In the Colts' preseason matchup against the Falcons on Saturday, Shrader nailed both of his field goal attempts (48 and 53 yards), while Grupe missed a 37-yard attempt wide right.
Shrader is now 4-for-4 on field goal attempts (long of 61) during preseason play, whereas Grupe is now 0-for-2.

title: Winners and Losers From Colts Joint Practices vs. Falcons
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts wrapped up their ninth and final training camp at Grand Park Sports Campus this week with two joint practices with the Atlanta Falcons.
The Colts performed like the better team throughout the two practices. Both sides of the ball racked up their fair share of wins against a Falcons team that is full of questions.
Here are the winners and losers from the joint practices.
Daniel Jones has been wildly impressive throughout training camp, and that continued against the Falcons this week.
Jones was a perfect 15-of-15 passing in Wednesday's practice as the Falcons had no answers for the Colts' passing attack. While he came back down to earth on Thursday, going 3-of-4 in 11-on-11 drills, Jones still led a scoring drive in a two-minute situation in the final period of the day.
It's hard to imagine what more Jones could have done during training camp. Indy's QB1 looks as sharp as ever, showing off pinpoint accuracy and a command of the offense. Jones is still less than nine months removed from tearing his Achilles, yet the injury seems like an afterthought at this point due to his level of play.
While Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward Sr. are the big names amongst the cornerback group, it has been Justin Walley who has made the most highlight plays. Walley continued his standout camp against the Falcons, battling with Pro Bowl wide receiver Drake London on numerous occasions.
While London made a highlight grab over Walley on Wednesday, the second-year cornerback responded on Thursday with a crucial pass breakup in 7-on-7 work and a would-be pick-6 in 11-on-11s. Walley's playmaking ability has become a regular occurrence in training camp, and the Colts believe it will translate to Sundays as well.
While Lou Anarumo has been rotating the linebacker group most of training camp, Jaylon Carlies was with the starting defense for both joint practices. Carlies had a strong showing in the preseason opener and continued to make plays against the Falcons .
Carlies came up with an interception of Michael Penix Jr. in 7-on-7s that fired up the defense. Carlies also made an impact as a blitzer, forcing Tua Tagovailoa into a few bad throws. The young linebacker is finally healthy and ascending at the right time, and it may lead to a starting role in the regular season.
If there was one area that the Colts struggled with against the Falcons, it was the running game . None of Jonathan Taylor, Seth McGowan, or Ulysses Bentley IV could find much running room behind the Colts' offensive line. The Falcons did a great job getting off of their blocks and meeting the Colts' running backs at or behind the line of scrimmage.
The Colts definitely have some things to clean up in their ground attack. It is hard to get a full read of the running game in practice when there is no tackling. Regardless, the Colts will need to be a threat on the ground with Taylor and the offensive line if the offense is to replicate last season's success.
Tyler Warren has been one of the standouts of training camp and was poised to continue his dominance against the Falcons' defense. Unfortunately for Warren, the Pro Bowl tight end slipped and injured his groin during a drill at the beginning of Wednesday's practice. Warren did not practice on Thursday as a result.
Fortunately, Warren seems to have escaped serious injury and is expected to miss only a week's worth of action. The Colts should have their tight end back and healthy for their Week 1 matchup with the Baltimore Ravens. Warren is expected to be a massive part of the Colts' offense this season and looks ready to ascend amongst the elite at his position.

title: 3 Things We Learned From Jaguars' First Joint Practice With Buccaneers: Travis Hunter's Time
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have one more joint practice left with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but there was plenty of action from Day 1 still worth examining.
So, what did we learn from the Jaguars' first joint practice against the Buccaneers on Tuesday at the Miller Electric Center? We take a look at it all below.
We expected Travis Hunter to stick at cornerback for the duration of Tuesday's practice, and that is exactly what happened. Hunter has spent most of the last 10 days or so at cornerback, taking few reps with the offense at wide receiver after splitting his time between the two spots during the first few legs of training camp. Even with injuries to Brian Thomas Jr., Jakobi Meyers, and Parker Washington at different times, the Jaguars have kept Hunter at cornerback in practice.
I do not think this is a reflection of what Hunter's role on offense will be. And in the event the Jaguars sustain wide receiver injuries during the season, I do think Hunter would see an increased role on offense instead of the Jaguars turning to Josh Cameron, CJ Williams, and Austin Trammell instead. But what this is a reflection of is the fact that the Jaguars are making it crystal clear that Hunter is CB1. They believe his reps are better served on defense after a limited scope there as a rookie, and that is where he will major when it comes to Week 1.
"The chemistry between that group back there is so important, and so yes, I do think we have absolutely made progress. Are we there yet? No, just hasn't played a lot of football in the last nine months or whatever it's been," Coen said Tuesday.
"So, I've been pleased with his intentionality. I've been pleased with the group as a whole in terms of really working together. I think they're a close-knit group as a whole, and with him not being in the fold as much, especially towards the back half of the year, he just missed out on a lot of things, a lot of communication, a lot of continuity, and so that's something that we've been working to continue to build on. And I have been pleased with the development, but we need more. We need as much work as we can get.”
This is the time in training camp where there is no longer value in the Jaguars trying out different offensive line combinations for the sake of reps and insurance purposes. It sure feels like that, outside of the status of Cole Van Lanen at right tackle, the Jaguars have shown us who their starting offensive line is, and the headliner is rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon starting at left guard.
The Jaguars clearly see him as one of their best five not just because he has gotten extensive reps with the first-team over the last week, but they also moved long-time left guard Ezra Cleveland to right guard instead of keeping him on the left side and starting Wyatt Milum at right guard. Pregnon is here to stay, and the practice reps he is getting alongside Trevor Lawrence, Anton Harrison, Robert Hainsey and the rest of the starters is only making this more clear.
Both Jaguars running backs performed when called upon, but it was Chris Rodriguez Jr.'s role that especially stood out to me. Rodriguez and Bhayshul Tuten got seemingly equal reps throughout the entire practice, but when the Jaguars went with their end-of-game drill during the final period of practice, it was Rodriguez who got the nod at running back. This mostly meant pass-protection for Lawrence and the Jaguars' passing game, though the Jaguars also threw a screen to Rodriguez early on in the drive.
So, why does this matter? Because as things stand today, the Jaguars are still without passing-down running back LeQuint Allen. The second-year running back is set to miss the rest of camp with a soft tissue injury and it remains to be seen exactly when he will return. That means there is a clear void when it comes to the passing down depth chart, because that is a role Allen dominated for the Jaguars.
I said in our latest mailbag that I think Rodriguez is the Jaguars' best pass-protecting running back with Allen injured. The fact the Jaguars put him on the field for a two-minute drive over Tuten indicates that they agree,

title: 8 Winners, 4 Losers From Day 19 of Jaguars Training Camp: Parker Washington Gets a Boost
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Day 19 of training camp brought plenty of good moments for the Jacksonville Jaguars, though not everyone can be a winner.
So, who are the winners and losers from the joint practice with the Buccaneers? We take a look below.
With Brian Thomas Jr. out for most of the day and Jakobi Meyers also out, most of the Jaguars' passing game predictably flowed through Parker Washington. There were a few moments where he and Trevor Lawrence were just a tick off and didn't come through on the completion, but there were even more moments where Washington got open at each level of the field for chunk gains. Washington is my pick for Jaguars leading receiver after what we have seen over the course of training camp.
If Tuesday's practice was a game, Josh Hines-Allen could have set a career-high in single-game sacks. He was arguably the best player on the field , and the Jaguars were able to see the rest of the defensive line thrive off his energy and impact. It feels like Hines-Allen is on the verge of a special year, because he continues to look like a terror for opposing offensive lines each time he lines up against them this summer.
If Washington was the Jaguars' most-targeted receiver on Tuesday, then Brenton Strange was not far behind him. The Jaguars' big-money tight end made a few big catches downfield on the day, such as the one below. With that said, I think his best catch came on a middle of the field contested catch from Trevor Lawrence between two defenders that showed why he is a safe go-to target in gotta have it situations.
That boy @BrentonStrange ! 👀 Grab tickets to #TBvsJAX : https://t.co/XnjmMS4q7M @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/kxDd1HDmEb
Tuesday might have been the best practice that Montaric Brown has had this summer. The reliable starting cornerback can be depended on as much as any other starter on the Jaguars' defense thanks to his consistency, but he also looked like a bonafide playmaker against the Buccaneers' passing game. Brown recorded an interception against Baker Mayfield and was able to swarm around the football all day. Brown is going to be one of the most important pieces on the entire defense this season, and Tuesday was an encouraging step.
Liam Coen made it very clear after last week's preseason game against the Panthers that both Ventrell Miller and Branson Combs will see snaps on defense this year, regardless of who starts off the game on the field. With that said, Miller is still going to be listed as a winner here for a few different reasons. For one, he seemed to be the linebacker who got the most reps alongside Foyesade Oluokun on the day, which still has to count for something. Secondly, Miller was a force against the run and made a few plays that showed why the Jaguars are so high on him as a downhill defender. He has a chance to carve out a nice role in Anthony Campanile's defense this season.
The Jaguars' running back duo keeps stacking good performances in joint practices. Both Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. had impressive runs against the Buccaneers' defense, with Tuten showing off home run ability and Rodriguez churning out some tough additional yards on seemngly every touch. Tuten had a fumble early, but the Jaguars did not shy away from getting him the ball after that.
Emmanuel Pregnon seemed like he was able to meet the moment for the Jaguars' offensive line. It was not a perfect day for either him or the unit, but it seems like the upside continues to show the more and more he gets reps alongside the rest of the first-team offense. He is starting to look more like the favorite to start at left guard in Week 1 against the Cleveland Browns with each practice the Jaguars hold.
“I saw him on one play. Where I think he drove somebody down the field a good bit and finished. That was the only real play that I guess I noticed him on. I have to go and watch this tape and see. I didn't feel like out there it was too big for him," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after practice. " I didn't feel like there was a physical mismatch or a mental ‘man, this is too fast for me.’ Obviously, have to go take a look. I've been pleased with his development thus far, and hopefully, he can continue to trend up.”
I know. Baker Mayfield is not a Jacksonville Jaguar and you could generally not care less about him. With that said, he had what I thought was a fairly brutal day as far as joint August practices go. Bryce Young was better for the Carolina Panthers a week before, and Mayfield himself said after practice that the Jaguars more or less bullied the Buccaneers on Tuesday. The further we get from Liam Coen's exit from Tampa Bay, the more it looks like Coen was that offense's most important piece.
Bucs QB Baker Mayfield said Jacksonville was playing with “their hair on fire” and said had it been a game today; his team would not have been on the winning side. pic.twitter.com/GRpGpnEWTO
It felt like Brian Thomas Jr. was about to have a terrific outing against the Buccaneers . He produced the most explosive play of the day for either team on the very first play from scrimmage with his deep touchdown, but he landed on his shoulder on the play and only had one more rep until he was sidelined for the rest of the day. The Jaguars are rightfully playing it safe with Thomas, but it seemed like an injury was the only thing stopping him from a big performance on Tuesday.
Trevor Lawrence himself had a good day against the Buccaneers, and he didn't put the football in harm's way once. But man, did he feel unlucky. He lost Brian Thomas Jr. after one terrific connection, had two rookie receivers and a few other backups like Tim Jones, Austin Trammell, and Brady Boyd running with the offense all afternoon, and was on the wrong end of a few drops from the receivers. The offense stalled out on the last drive of the day, and it felt like Lawrence was a victim in that result as much as anything else.
Count me as a fan of Tampa Bay Buccaneers pass-rusher Rueben Bain Jr, but even I did not think he would take over Tuesday's practice at the frequency that he did. He was a problem for the Jaguars throughout the afternoon and it seemed like he was able to tee off against multiple Jaguars' tackles not named Anton Harrison.

title: Good and Not So Good From Day 19 of Jaguars Training Camp: Josh Hines-Allen Takes Over
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars held their third of four joint practices on Tuesday, and it was an eventful day at the Miller Electric Center.
So, what were the highs and the lows of Day 19 of training camp? Who stepped up the most, and what issues flared up? We break it down below with The Good and The Not So Good from the first day of joint practices with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
The Jaguars' defensive line as a whole has been impressive in joint practices this summer, but they took it arguably to another level against the Buccaneers. That effort was mostly led by defensive end Josh Hines-Allen, who broke the franchise sack record last season and who certainly looks prepared for another big year. A lot of what the Jaguars' rush does is built upon Hines-Allen's skill-set, and this was crystal clear with his performance setting the tone for the unit on Tuesday.
“Man, Josh, he had a hell of a day, which that's typical," Jaguars defensive end Travon Walker said after practice. "He's one of those, you know he's going to come into practice ready to work every day, and he just continuously keeps growing and keeps working on his craft every day, and it showed today.
It felt like the Jaguars secondary had been getting tested in joint practices before Tuesday's, but Day 19 of camp felt like the best evidence of secondary improvement the Jaguars have put on display all summer. It wasn't just because Travis Hunter focused on defense, either. Hunter recorded a pass breakup on the day, but this felt more like a team-effort with the likes of Buster Brown, Jarrian Jones, Antonio Johnson, Eric Murray, Jalen Huskey, and Caleb Ransaw all getting their hands on passes at one point or another.
The Buccaneers' passing game felt frustrated for much of the day, and Brown in particular had a strong performance to cause that kind of stress. The Jaguars' secondary and overall scheme has evolved compared to last year, and there were some positive steps taken in that endeavor on Tuesday.
“Yeah, that's a big thing that we've been working on this offseason has been, challenging people a little bit more, eliminating some of the easy completions that might have hurt us at times last year, and really understanding situation football for Buster as well," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after practice.
"Like understanding the down and distance and what the call is, understanding in the red zone what type of routes that you're going to be typically having to defend, and so it was nice, great to see us get our hands on a few because we haven't had a ton of ball disruption as much as we'd like to maybe have, and that's the yin and yang. You play a little bit more match coverage. Well, your eyes are on the receiver, not the quarterback, so that's always the balance. It's like, do we want to get more sacks and ball production in terms of challenging routes, or do you want to sit there in vision zone and get picked apart, but you're going to get some turnovers, so that's something that we've been working through.”
I thought the Jaguars had a strong day in terms of performances from their young players. A few rookies made plays over the day, but I think it was the second-year Jaguars who had an even better day.
I thought the Jaguars did a great job of keeping Trevor Lawrence clean in the practice against the Panthers, but they did not have as much luck on Tuesday. Some of the more impressive throws Lawrence made on the day, including a dazzling touchdown pass to Parker Washington, would have been sacks in a game, and it seemed like the Jaguars were allowing the pressure from a few different spots.
The Buccaneers do have a quality front, and their scheme can be a difficult one to play against without a week of game-planning for it. But Lawrence was too often in the crosshairs of the Buccaneers' pass-rushers on Tuesday, and that was despite the Jaguars having most of their offensive line back from injuries.
The Jaguars saw rookie wide receivers Josh Cameron and CJ Williams spend the day with the first-team offense due to injuries at the position, and the offense predictably looked like a unit that had rookies in the place of experienced veterans like Brian Thomas Jr. and Jakobi Meyers. This especially showed up when the Jaguars' offense stalled out on their final drive of the day.
Cameron did make a few quality plays on the day, but Tuesday felt like a day in which the offense started and stalled a few different times over the course of the afternoon. The reasonable explanation for that was because it was a bigger workload for the youngest players in the room.
"There were a couple things that I think we might have jacked up out there. I know they're blocking their tails off. I know Josh had a couple good ones," Coen said after practice.
"Probably didn't get a ton of like target work. Parker [WR Parker Washington] was probably getting a lot of it. Strange [TE Brenton Strange] got some more, but I've been pleased with their ability to jump in, in terms of Jakobi’s [WR Jakobi Meyers] down, then B.T.'s [WR Brain Thomas Jr.] out. Being able to go in and us still operate as an offense and still be able to be efficient at times. Still like to see us separate maybe a little bit better on some of those second-level throws, but they're coming along.”
With Brian Thomas Jr. landing on his shoulder on the first play of the practice, the Jaguars went through the day without him and Jakobi Meyers. That left quite the void in the wide receiver room, and one that will probably not get much action until the first week of practice during the regular-season. The Jaguars' passing game can survive in the very short-term, but there will be some moving pieces until then.

title: Everything I Saw at Day 19 of Jaguars Training Camp: Defense Thumps Buccaneers
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars held their first of two joint practices with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Tuesday, and it was another camp practice filled with some good, some bad, and plenty in between.
So, what did we see from the Jaguars in their joint practice vs. the Buccaneers? We break it down below.
The Jaguars did not create any takeaways in their first two joint practices this summer, with the New Orleans Saints finding some offensive success against them two weeks ago, and with the Carolina Panthers avoiding any game-changing mistakes the week before. That changed against the Buccaneers, however, with the Jaguars getting four takeaways by my count.
The first takeaway happened in the red-zone, with Jaguars safety Eric Murray crashing down on Buccaneers tight end Payne Durham to force a fumble, which was recovered by Foyesade Oluokun for an early tone-setting play. The Buccaneers did not find much success early on in practice on offense in general outside of targeting rookie wide receiver Ted Hurst.
The second takeaway was an athletic play from Buster Brown, who had perhaps his best practice of training camp. Brown, who also recorded a tackle for loss in the run game, was able to nab a Baker Mayfield pass out of the air for a big turnover in team drills.
🗣️ Put some respect on Buster Brown! Grab tickets to #TBvsJAX : https://t.co/XnjmMS4q7M @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/gHCA2a2rzO
The third takeaway was a punch-out forced fumble by defensive end B.J. Green, who flew screaming to the sideline on a screen and made an excellent effort play. The final takeaway of the day then came from Antonio Johnson, who had an easy pick-six on Mayfield where the closest Buccaneers receivers were located in Gainseville, for some reason. This ended a end-of-game period where the Jaguars' defensive dominated Tampa's offense. It was a good day for Anthony Campanile's unit.
I thought coming into practice that Brian Thomas Jr. was due for a big, big day. It only took one play into scrimmage for Thomas to make an impact, too, with the third-year receiver beating Buccaneers cornerback Zyon McCollum downfield for a 50+ yard touchdown pass from Trevor Lawrence. Thomas dived for the pass and was able to secure it for the score, but he did land hard on his left shoulder and clearly felt some discomfort coming off the field after the play.
Thomas went back in for one play (that he was not targeted on), and then his day was over. Trainers looked at him for a few minutes before he sat out the rest of practice alongside Jakobi Meyers, though he did remain on the sidelines and in his pads. Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said he thinks Thomas is "alright" after the injury, and the Jaguars will need to hope that he is right. Thomas has had a good camp, and now the focus will have to turn to making sure he is ready for Week 1.
With both Thomas and Meyers not practicing, the Jaguars had rookie receivers Josh Cameron and CJ Williams get reps with the 1s. Williams had a tough day, but Cameron had several catches delivered by a pass from Lawrence, including a big first down at the end-of-game period and a touchdown in the red-zone.
For my money, there was clearly one player on the field on Tuesday who was a step above everyone else: Jaguars defensive end Josh Hines-Allen had the kind of practice that Liam Coen so often talks about, disrupting enough of the Buccaneers offense that it would have been warranted for a stoppage in the fight. Whether agaisnt the run or the pass, Hines-Allen worked both Buccaneers offensive tackles and seemingly got into the backfield at will.
41 off the edge, that's a scary sight 🫣 @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/hZUK0V9eNV
Hines-Allen is entering his eigth season and it is clear the days of him having to put in an entire summer's worth of dominant practices are over. We know he is an elite pass-rusher, and he turns it on once Week 1 comes around or once he has a non-Jaguars lineman in front of him. That is exactly what happened on Tuesday, with Hines-Allen looking like a force for most of the day and recording at least two sacks and a handful of other pressures.
I did not think the Jaguars' offense was quite as sharp as it was the week before against the Panthers, but it had its moments. Here were the down parts of the day: Williams had a few passes go off his hands, Brady Boyd and Tim Jones each failed to haul in passes from Lawrence, Bhayshul Tuten had an early fumble (his first of camp), and I thought the Jaguars gave up a lot more pressure this week than they did against the Panthers, especially along the right side of the offensive line.
As for the good: Coen said after practice that he was happy with Tuten's day, with the second-year back hitting several explosive runs. Chris Rodriguez Jr. had an efficient day, Emmanuel Pregnon continued to look steady at left guard, and Brenton Strange and Parker Washington each made big grabs downfield while also serving as the focal points of the passing game for the day.
The Jaguars were missing two starting receivers for more or less the entire practice and, at times, looked like it. But they still made plays, and Washington still looked mostly uncoverable at all levels of the field.
While it certainly felt like some bad luck that Thomas got injured after the play, his catch against McCollum for a touchdown on the first play from scrimmage was the kind of play that would be a regular on a SportsCenter Top 10. Thomas has always performed well against the Buccaneers in this setting, and today was no different.

title: 5 Jaguars to Watch in Joint Practices vs. Buccaneers: Brian Thomas Jr.'s Time
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are set to enter the last two days of training camp on Tuesday and Wednesday, and each day is sure to have plenty of action thanks to the visiting Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
So, which Jaguars will we keep our eyes on the closest during the pair of joint practices with the Buccaneers? We break it down below.
Jaguars veteran receiver Brian Thomas Jr. has always been a star in joint practices; he broke out in his rookie training camp with a stellar performance against the Buccaneers, performed well in last year's practice against the Miami Dolphins, and has once again thrived in the Jaguars' joint practices in 2026. With Jakobi Meyers' status up in the air, Thomas should also get plenty of volume alongside Parker Washington.
Thomas has built plenty of momentum entering Week 1, with the third-year wideout's connection with Trevor Lawrence seeming to improve not just downfield, but also in the intermediate part of the field. Another big practice against the Buccaneers should solidify that upward trend entering Week 1's bout with the Cleveland Browns.
It would be a shock if the Jaguars' first-team offensive line does not continue to have Emmanuel Pregnon at left guard this week. Pregnon impressed with the promotion last week, and the Jaguars have kept him there in recent practice days even with the return of multiple offensive linemen from injuries. Signs are pointing toward Pregnon starting in Week 1, which means the Buccaneers will be his last real test before then.
Pregnon has displayed great power as a run-defender and has been stout in pass-protection, but Tampa Bay's defense will likely test different parts of his game. His ability to diagnose blitzes and pass-rush games that the Buccaneers throw at the Jaguars could be the greatest sign yet of whether he is truly ready to be a Week 1 starter.
I thought Travon Walker was extremely disruptive in last week's joint practice against the Panthers, but the Buccaneers should offer a much better test. The Buccaneers' offensive line is a few tiers above where the Panthers are at, plus they have a big-money duo at offensive tackle that should test the Jaguars' pass-rush. Walker has had probably the best camp he has ever had just in terms of pure disruption, and continuing this against the Buccaneers would be an impressive step.
I would expect Walker's role this season to see him moved around the defensive front a bit more, so watching him work against the Buccaneers' offensive line from a variety of alignments will be fascinating. He has all of the traits to be a game-wrecker for any offense, and he has the potential to do it in this week's practices.
It seems safe to say that we are going to see Travis Hunter at cornerback for the duration of this week's practices. Going against a passing game and skill group that has been highly productive in the past should be a great test for Hunter ahead of Week 1, which will likely be the game in which he sees his biggest exposure to cornerback yet in his NFL career.
Hunter has the talent to be one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL and he had some impressive showings vs. Tetairoa McMillan last week. The Jaguars need to make more big plays in the secondary, and he feels like he is their best hope to doing that, both in this week's practices and when the regular season begins.
Jaguars rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher caught a touchdown against the Panthers last week and had some highs and lows as a blocker against an impressive edge group. What kind of step he takes in both areas against the Buccaneers could indicate to us how ready he is to make a Week 1 impact in Liam Coen's offense.
Boerkircher will likely see Rueben Bain in a few reps in the running game, and I am interested to see how he holds up after a few losses in the run game last week. As a pass-catcher, he will be facing a better secondary this week than a week ago, so his performance in the red-zone will be notable.

title: 3 Things That Will Really Matter When Jaguars Practice vs. Buccaneers
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will hold their final two practices of training camp on Tuesday and Wednesday, and they will have some guests.
After visiting the New Orleans Saints for a joint practice two weeks ago and hosting the Carolina Panthers last week, t he Jaguars are set to play host yet again this week with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
So, what will we be watching the closest when the Jaguars and Buccaneers clash on the practice field? We break it down below.
Emmanuel Pregnon has kicked off a second week in a row with the Jaguars' first team at left guard, and this week's slate of practices against a talented Buccaneers front could tell us just how ready he is to be a rookie starter. As Jaguars head coach Liam Coen noted on Sunday, Pregnon and the Jaguars will be facing a much different scheme this week than the previous two joint practices, which will give us another data point for Pregnon's case to be a starter.
“I think this will be a good test. I think this will be a nice test this week. Todd [Bowles] and their defense, they throw a lot of different looks at you," Coen said.
"Last week in Carolina and in New Orleans was a little bit more of a similar defense to each other. Less pressure, stunts, twists, movement so that was great to get him kind of going. Now, this is going to be a little bit of a test in terms of being able to, handle all that: the communication, the moving parts, the picks, the stunts, the twists, the pressures. I think this will be a great op for us to be able to really work with him and work through this week and hopefully he continues to ascend.”
If Pregnon can impress this week like he did a week ago, he could very well wrap up the starting left guard spot for Week 1 vs. the Cleveland Browns. That is quite the climb for a rookie third-round pick, but he has done nothing but earn it.
The Jaguars' secondary was a big area of focus this offseason, and there is good reason the Jaguars have seen Travis Hunter spend the vast majority of his reps over the last week at cornerback. Hunter practiced more defense than offense over the first dozen or so Jaguars training camp practices, but not by the gap that he has in recent practices. He did not spend a single 11-on-11 rep on offense on Sunday for example , and spent most of the joint practice with the Panthers on defense.
Hunter has had some wow-level reps at cornerback this summer, and he seemed to match up well with Tetairoa McMillan a week ago. If he can put together another productive outing against a talented Buccaneers unit, then all arrows will be pointing upward as the Jaguars prepare for him to be their top cornerback in Week 1.
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said he is excited to see Jaguars defensive end Josh Hines-Allen matchup with Buccaneers offensive tackles Tristan Wirds and Luke Goedeke, and he isn't alone. Hines-Allen, Travon Walker and Arik Armstead seemingly dominated last week's joint practice with the Panthers, but the Buccaneers' offensive line is a different animal entirely.
The Panthers might have a bottom-five offensive line in football, and they have the type of unit that the Jaguars' star-studded defensive line should find success against. The Buccaneers are in  a different tier altogether, however, and they should provide a good test for just how good the Jaguars' pass-rush is.

title: Tony Boselli’s New NFL Appointment Could Be a Big Win for the Jaguars
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Jacksonville Jaguars Executive Vice President of Football Operations Tony Boselli has an important new role.
The Jaguars' legend was named to the NFL Competition Committee on Monday afternoon, landing the Hall of Famer an important appointment within the NFL.
"I have always viewed the game of football – and the institutions and traditions that support it – as sacred," Boselli said in a statement. "I felt that way when I entered the National Football League as a player more than 30 years ago, and I feel an even greater responsibility to it today.
"It is an honor to serve on the Competition Committee and to represent the best interests of the game, the NFL, and all 32 clubs. I look forward to joining the other members of the committee and continuing their good work as we thoroughly study the game, protect its integrity, and continue to evolve and grow it for future generations of players and fans."
Boselli's appointment to the committee is a big honor, with former commissioner Pete Rozelle created the competition committee in 1968. But why could this honor also equate to good news for the Jaguars at large?
Simply put, Boselli will now be one of the voices on the most important NFL committee today. The competition committee "reviews all competitive aspects of the game, including (but not limited to) playing rules, roster regulations, technology, game-day operations and player protection," and is overseen by co-chairmen Stephen Jones and Rich McKay.
Other members of the committee include Katie Blackburn (Cincinnati Bengals), Todd Bowles (Tampa Bay Buccaneers), John Lynch (San Francisco 49ers), John Mara (New York Giants), Sean McVay (Los Angeles Rams) , Kevin O'Connell (Minnesota Vikings), Sean Payton (Denver Broncos), DeMeco Ryans (Houston Texans), and Mike Vrabel (New England Patriots). This is a short list of the NFL's who's who, with only a few key names missing.
By virtue of Boselli rubbing shoulders with so many top head coaches and executives around the league, this offers the Jaguars yet another chance to expand their relationships and influence around the NFL. Having a voice with keen understanding of the questions facing the franchise on the committee is undoubtedly a good thing for Jacksonville, but the relationships with the rest of the committee might be the biggest draw.
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen noted during the offseason that the Jaguars wanted more joint practices in 2025, for example, but it didn't happen due to the newness the Jaguars' fresh regime offered.
"Last year we were in a first-year spot, so we didn't get a ton of juice and help on that front, so we ended up having one joint practice against Miami and that was it in [Preseason] Week 3," Coen said in March.
This time around, the Jaguars have scheduled four joint practices across three weeks with all three opponents, which has directly impacted how they have deployed players in the preseason. The extra juice and influence from the franchise paid off, and that is just one example of how Boselli's new role could help the Jaguars. Whenever the Jaguars need to connect with several of the NFL's top franchises, they now have an easy in.

title: 6 Jaguars Veterans On the Bubble Entering Final Week of Training Camp
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will have to make some tough decisions this week.
With training camp entering its final leg, teams will have to make massive roster cuts on Sunday afternoon as they trim each roster to 53 players. For the Jaguars, that could mean trouble for a few veterans who have been able to carve out roles on past rosters. Here are six who may fall into that category.
It would not make much sense for the Jaguars to keep both Jalen McLeod and Yasir Abdullah, unless the Jaguars opt to not move forward with Jahlani Tavai as a backup off-ball linebacker following the season-ending injury to Parker Hughes. With the role that the strong side linebacker players in Anthony Campanile's scheme, though, history suggests there will be one winner from this battle.
Abdullah started off the preseason strong with a sack and a stellar special teams tackle in Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints, though he was less successful against the Carolina Panthers last week. Jalen McLeod did not play in the first two preseason games, but returned to practice this week and should be expected to play in the preseason finale against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
McLeod has flashed some real upside as a pass-rusher earlier in training camp, and the 2025 Day 3 pick seemed to be building momentum. Abdullah is an experienced pro, though, and offers proven special teams value. This one feels like it could go either way.
Perhaps I am reading the situation wrongly and I should include Jabbar Muhammad alongside Christian Braswell. With that said, I do feel like Muhammad has done enough to win the No. 5 cornerback job for the Jaguars, which would mean Braswell would need the Jaguars to carry six cornerbacks in order to make the roster yet again.
With that said, Braswell does have the upside of experience with the coaching staff. The Jaguars staff loved what he brought to the table on defense and special teams last season, and he has returned to the field after being limited at the start of training camp.
“Yeah, Bras, he's done a great job to fight his way back. That's kind of who he is, though too," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said Monday. "He's a guy who gives you maximum effort. He's a high-character guy. He's got a ton of talent. He's an explosive guy, whether that's on special teams or defense, he's been a guy that we can rely on. It's good to get him back, where he's feeling good and watch him get out there and run around a little bit."
When the Jacksonville Jaguars drafted rookie tight ends Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol in April, they made it clear that it would be hard for many other veteran tight ends not named Brenton Strange to make the roster. The Jaguars could easily carry four tight ends, but five would seem like a big stretch. That means there could be one spot to be split between Hunter Long and Quintin Morris, and that is only in the scenario in which the Jaguars do carry four tight ends.
Morris was more effective than Long last season, though Long has had a better training camp in 2026. This could ultimately come down to special teams value, or the Jaguars could go with just the rookies and Brenton Strange at one of their most-changed position groups to date.
It has been an interesting situation when it comes to the final spot on the Jaguars' offensive line. The Jaguars returned all nine of the top offensive linemen from the 2025 squad and also added Emmanuel Pregnon to the mix. With that in mind, the Jaguars entered camp with an injury question with Cole Van Lanen, which created the question of whether an extra offensive lineman could start the season on the roster while the Jaguars waited on Van Lanen.
Then the Jaguars' offensive line took another hit with guard Patrick Mekari , who reportedly underwent back surgery and is on an unknown time table. Chuma Edoga seemed like a lock for the 53-man roster at that point, but then the Jaguars started to get some reinforcements in the form of a trade for Daniel Faalele and Van Lanen being activated off the Active/PUP list.
That now means there is once again a logjam at the No. 9 and No. 10 spot. It is hard to imagine Edoga is over any Walker Little, Wyatt Milum, Jonah Monheim, or Faalele if the Jaguars keep only nine offensive linemen, which could mean a tough departure for the veteran backup.

title: 1 Sleeper Who Could Completely Shake Up Jaguars' 53-Man Roster
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- When it comes to the Jacksonville Jaguars' roster, there doesn't expect to be many surprises waiting ahead on Sunday's cut down day. But that doesn't mean there are none .
The Jaguars' 53-man roster will be a tough one to crack for any sleeper, simply based on the fact that the Jaguars brought back most of last year's roster while also adding double-digit draft picks, nine of which are eligible for this year's active roster.
But there is one name who has continued to make a case for himself: undrafted rookie defensive end Bryan Thomas Jr. , who is continuing to become a difficult sleeper to keep off the roster.
Dubbed as "the other BTJ" on the Jaguars' roster, Bryan Thomas Jr. has flashed ever since the Jaguars added him following the 2026 NFL Draft. That is why he has a fighting chance to make the Jaguars' roster, even with their other investments at the position.
“He definitely has shown me some things," Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said Monday. "He's played explosively in the games, and I think he's jumped out. His play style, his effort, that's jumped out. And that's what we saw in him watching his tape at South Carolina."
Thomas is one of multiple rookie defensive ends on the roster, joining Day 3 picks Wesley Williams and Zach Durfee, along with fellow undrafted rookie defensive end 
Quindarius Dunnigan. Thomas' college skill-set and production certainly stood out to Jacksonville, with the rookie pass-rusher playing in 46 games (19 starts) over four seasons at South Carolina (2022-25)
.
In that time, he recorded92 career tackles (52 solo), 18.5 tackles for loss, 12.5 sacks and five forced fumbles and earned All-SEC Third-Team honors in 2025. He succeeded there for the same reasons he has continued to flash for the Jaguars, and Campanile has noticed.
"He was a guy that was going to run and hit. He was going to play his ass off every play," Campanile said. "That's what, honestly, we really liked about him and we were fired up to get him in here for that reason. He's proven to do that here in the summer and since the spring, since he's been here.”
Thomas has seemingly been racking up pressures at will over the first two weeks of the preseason, showing similar preseason flashes as B.J. Green and Danny Striggow did in the same position a year ago. Thomas has even more competition than them to make the roster, though, and it very well could come down to him or Durfee for the final spot.
“I mean, they can come in and play and make plays immediately. Obviously, you can tell just by putting on the tape, man, we have a lot of young guys that are proving themselves. There’s not a lot of spots to fill," Jaguars defensive end Josh Hines-Allen said Sunday.
"And so, when you have a lot of great guys that are playing good football, especially young guys, who is going to be those one or two guys that are going to make the cut? And all those guys are battling for those one or two spots. It’s like that in a lot of different rooms as well. So, they're coming in with the right approach. And basically whoever plays better, whoever's the better football player is going to make this team, basically. But they all can make it. I'm just excited to see what that final cut's going to be. I'm going to be upset to see what that final cut's going to be, and just got to take it the way it is.”
